867.note: Europe in 867: the Carolingian realms are ruled by Charles the Bald, Louis the German and Lothair II; Great Moravia is under Rastislav; the Magyar confederation remains east of the Carpathian Basin; and the Great Heathen Army is campaigning in England. Iberian, Scandinavian and Balkan rulers are updated to the period. The map reuses modern administrative regions as approximate historical proxies.

properties.info: Charles the Bald ruled West Francia in 867. The kingdom was a Carolingian realm whose powerful counts and regional rulers exercised substantial autonomy. Modern French regions are broad map proxies, not historical borders.

Louis the German ruled East Francia in 867. The kingdom comprised powerful duchies and frontier regions; modern German, Austrian and Slovenian administrative regions are only broad proxies, not historical borders.

Lothair II ruled the Middle Frankish kingdom of Lotharingia in 867. His realm occupied the lands between West and East Francia and included the western Alpine area shown here using modern Swiss cantons. The exact borders and local allegiances were fluid.

properties.label: Provence
properties.leader: Lothair II and Louis II (partitioned authority)
properties.info: The lands later grouped as Provence were divided after Charles of Provence's death in 863, with authority shared between Lothair II and Louis II. This layer uses later southern French regions as an approximate proxy for a contested Carolingian territory.

Louis II ruled the Kingdom of Italy in 867 and was also emperor. His authority was strongest in northern and central Italy; local rulers held much of the south. Modern Italian regions are broad map proxies.

properties.label: Great Moravia
properties.info: Great Moravia was a powerful Slavic polity under Rastislav in 867, before its decline following Frankish intervention in 870. Modern Slovakia and Moravia are used as approximate map proxies; the realm's wider influence was not a fixed border.

properties.label: Carpathian frontier
properties.info: In 867 the Magyar confederation was still east of the Carpathian Basin; its migration into the basin occurred later in the ninth century. This inherited area is therefore shown as a broad frontier of local Slavic and Avar-descended communities, not as a unified state.

Boris I ruled Bulgaria in 867. His reign saw the conversion of Bulgaria to Christianity and a major cultural transition. The map's broad Balkan frontier is approximate and should not be read as a precise boundary.

Basil I founded the Macedonian dynasty and became Byzantine emperor in 867. The empire held Greece, much of Anatolia and parts of southern Italy; its northern Balkan frontier shifted against Bulgaria. Modern regions are approximate map units.
Duke Domagoj ruled Croatia in the 860s. Croatia became a kingdom later in the tenth century; modern Croatian regions are approximate map proxies.
Mutimir ruled the Serbian principality in 867. Serbian rulers balanced between Byzantine and Bulgarian influence; the modern Serbian regions shown are approximate proxies rather than fixed borders.
The Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba was ruled by Muhammad I in 867. The caliphate was not proclaimed until 929. Its mapped extent is an approximation using modern Iberian regions.
Alfonso III ruled Asturias in 867. The kingdom was expanding southward, but its frontier with al-Andalus was fluid; modern northern Iberian provinces are approximate map proxies.
García Íñiguez ruled Pamplona around 867. The kingdom occupied a small and shifting Pyrenean sphere; modern provinces are approximate references.
Bernard of Gothia held the county of Barcelona in 867 as a royal appointee in the Carolingian frontier system. Local counts were gaining autonomy; modern provinces are map proxies.

Æthelred I was king of Wessex in 867. The Great Heathen Army had invaded England and was campaigning in Northumbria; Wessex, Mercia and the Danish-held areas are shown separately using modern counties as approximate proxies.

Burgred ruled Mercia in 867. The kingdom was under strong pressure from the Great Heathen Army but remained a distinct polity, closely allied with Wessex. Modern English counties are approximate proxies.

properties.leader: Danish army and local rulers; names uncertain
properties.info: The Great Heathen Army was active in eastern England in 867. Danish control and local leadership were unsettled; the modern county group is only an approximate map proxy.

properties.leader: Halfdan Ragnarsson and the Great Heathen Army
properties.info: The Great Heathen Army captured York in 866 and established Viking rule in Northumbria. Its territory and rulers remained contested; modern northern English counties are approximate proxies.
Constantine I ruled Alba from 862 to 877. The map retains the modern Scottish mainland as a rough proxy; the frontier and Norse influence in the north and west were fluid.
Seisyllwg was a Welsh kingdom under the dynasty of Rhodri Mawr. Its exact boundaries around 867 are uncertain; modern administrative areas are broad proxies.
Gwynedd was ruled by Anarawd ap Rhodri, son of Rhodri Mawr. Its extent is approximated with modern administrative areas.
Hywel ap Rhys ruled Morgannwg in the later ninth century. Its precise extent is uncertain; modern areas are shown only as broad proxies.

properties.leader: Local Svear and Götar rulers; names uncertain
properties.info: In 867, the areas later associated with Sweden were governed by regional rulers and assemblies; a unified kingdom and the identity of its rulers are uncertain. Existing modern regions are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Danish regional kings; no secure ruler for 867
properties.info: Denmark was divided among competing rulers in the ninth century; no securely established single king can be assigned to 867. The map uses southern Scandinavian regions as rough proxies.

properties.label: Norwegian petty kingdoms
properties.info: Norway had not yet been securely unified in 867. Later tradition associates Harald Fairhair with unification beginning around this period, but the chronology is debated. This layer represents a broad southern area of regional rulers, not one consolidated kingdom.

properties.label: Iceland
properties.info: The Norse settlement of Iceland is traditionally dated from around 874, so the Icelandic Commonwealth did not yet exist in 867. The island is retained as a geographic reference; earlier hermit settlement is possible but uncertain.

properties.label: Channel Islands
properties.info: The Norman duchy did not yet exist in 867. The islands are shown separately only as a geographic frontier; their political status at this date is uncertain.

properties.label: Pontic steppe
properties.info: In 867, Magyar groups lived in the Pontic steppe region before their later migration into the Carpathian Basin. This inherited frontier layer is only a broad geographic proxy and does not claim a unified steppe state.

properties.label: Early Rus'
properties.leader: Askold and Dir (according to later chronicles)
properties.info: Rus' groups were active around Kyiv by the mid-ninth century, including the raid on Constantinople in 860. Askold and Dir are known mainly from later chronicles; the broad Rus' network shown here should not be read as a consolidated Kievan state.

900.note: Around 900: Europe is reorganized around the West and East Frankish kingdoms, Lotharingia, Italy, the declining Great Moravian realm, the Magyar migration, the Bulgarian Empire, and the emerging Rus'. Iberia, the British Isles, Scandinavia, and the Balkans are also updated. This is a broad political reconstruction using modern province polygons as approximate map proxies, not historical borders; smaller frontier areas remain simplified.

properties.label: West Francia
properties.info: West Francia was a Carolingian kingdom ruled by Charles III in 900. Its counts and regional rulers exercised substantial autonomy. The map uses modern French administrative regions as broad proxies; Lotharingia and the Burgundian kingdoms are shown separately.

properties.label: East Francia
properties.info: East Francia was the eastern Carolingian kingdom, ruled by Louis the Child from 900. Its duchies and frontier territories had substantial local autonomy. The map uses modern German and Austrian regions as rough proxies; Lotharingia and Italy are shown separately.

properties.label: Channel Islands
properties.info: Around 900, the Channel Islands were not yet a Norman duchy. This map shows the islands as a Norse-influenced local area; their exact political status is uncertain.

properties.label: Upper Burgundy
properties.info: Upper Burgundy was a separate kingdom under Rudolf I in 900, centered on the western Alpine and Swiss lands. Its extent is approximated using modern Swiss cantons; these are not historical borders.
Swabia remained a major duchy in the East Frankish realm, although ducal authority was unsettled around 900. These eastern and central Swiss areas are retained as an approximate map proxy.

properties.label: West Slavic Lands
properties.info: Around 900, the Piast-led Kingdom of Poland had not yet formed. This layer represents West Slavic communities in the area using later Polish administrative regions as broad proxies; it does not imply a unified state.
Bohemia was ruled by the Přemyslid duke Spytihněv I around 900 and was closely connected to East Francia. Modern provinces are map references, not historical borders.

properties.label: Magyars
properties.info: The Magyar tribal confederation had entered the Carpathian Basin around 895 and was establishing itself there around 900. This map uses modern Hungarian regions and parts of Transylvania and the Danube frontier as broad proxies; the later Kingdom of Hungary did not yet exist.

properties.label: Croatia
properties.info: Croatia was ruled by Duke Muncimir around 900; it became a kingdom later in the tenth century. Modern Croatian regions are used as approximate map proxies.

Simeon I ruled Bulgaria from 893 and expanded its influence across the Balkans. This broad map retains the Bulgarian core and frontier areas; its borders with Byzantine and Serbian rulers were shifting and are not precise.

The Byzantine Empire was ruled by Leo VI in 900. It retained Greece, much of Anatolia and parts of southern Italy, while its northern Balkan frontier faced pressure from Bulgaria. Modern regions are approximate map units, not historical borders.

properties.label: Córdoba
properties.info: Al-Andalus was ruled by the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba in 900; the caliphate was proclaimed only in 929. The map retains the broad year-1000 territorial grouping as an approximation, with the northern Christian polities shown separately.

properties.label: Asturias
properties.info: In 900, the principal Christian kingdom in northwestern Iberia was Asturias. The Kingdom of León emerged after the division of Alfonso III's realm in 910. Existing provinces are broad proxies for the Christian north.
The Kingdom of Pamplona was ruled by Fortún Garcés around 900. The map uses later administrative provinces as approximate references for its western Pyrenean core.
The County of Barcelona was a frontier county of the Carolingian world, ruled by Wilfred II Borrell around 900. Its local rulers were increasingly autonomous; modern provinces are map proxies.
Denmark was consolidating as a kingdom around 900 under Gorm the Old. Scania and the southern Scandinavian regions are shown using modern boundaries as rough proxies.

Tradition associates Harald Fairhair with the gradual unification of Norway around this period, though its chronology and extent are debated. The map shows only a broad southern core; modern regions are not historical borders.

properties.leader: Early Swedish rulers; names and authority uncertain
properties.info: Around 900, the Swedish realm was still a developing polity centered on Svealand and Götaland. The extent and sequence of rulers are uncertain; the existing map is a broad regional proxy.

Oleg ruled the early Rus' polity from Kyiv after the capture of the city in 882. Around 900 it was an emerging dynastic state, not yet the later consolidated Kievan Rus'. The map retains a broad regional approximation.

properties.label: Wessex
properties.info: Wessex was the leading Anglo-Saxon kingdom around 900. Alfred the Great died in 899 and was succeeded by his son Edward. This map uses modern English administrative areas as broad proxies; Mercia, Danish Northumbria and Danish East Anglia are shown separately.
Constantine II ruled Alba from 900 to 943. The map retains the existing modern Scottish mainland proxy; Norse influence and the shifting frontier are not represented as precise borders.
Gwynedd was a leading Welsh kingdom around 900, ruled by Anarawd ap Rhodri. Its extent is approximated with modern administrative areas.
Powys remained a Welsh kingdom on the frontier with Mercia. Its ruler and exact extent around 900 are uncertain; modern areas are used as rough map proxies.

properties.label: Seisyllwg
properties.info: The later kingdom of Deheubarth had not yet been established around 900. This approximate layer uses the existing southwestern Welsh provinces as a proxy for Seisyllwg.
Morgannwg (Glywysing) was a Welsh polity in the southeast. Its precise extent and ruler around 900 are uncertain; modern areas are shown only as broad proxies.

properties.label: Lotharingia
properties.info: Lotharingia was a contested middle kingdom within the Carolingian world; Zwentibold's rule ended in 900, and the realm was subsequently disputed by East and West Francia. Modern Benelux, western German and northeastern French regions are approximate proxies.

properties.label: Italy
properties.info: Berengar I was king of Italy in 900, though his authority was contested. This approximate map assigns the northern and central Italian regions previously shown in the imperial sphere to the kingdom, while the Papal States and southern Italian polities remain separate.

properties.label: Provence
properties.info: The Kingdom of Lower Burgundy, often called Provence, was ruled by Louis the Blind around 900. This broad map uses the southern French regions of the later Burgundian grouping as proxies; borders were not fixed modern boundaries.

properties.label: Great Moravia
properties.info: Great Moravia was weakened by internal conflict and Magyar incursions after 894, but its political structures persisted into the early tenth century. This approximate layer uses modern Slovakia and Moravia; its former extent and control in 900 remain uncertain.

properties.label: Serbia
properties.info: Serbian principalities re-emerged between Byzantine and Bulgarian influence. Petar Gojniković ruled from the early tenth century; the map approximates the Serbian core with modern administrative regions, not fixed borders.

properties.label: Mercia
properties.info: Mercia remained a distinct polity under Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians, who acknowledged Alfred of Wessex as overlord. The map approximates its territory with modern administrative areas; its political status and frontier were more complex than a modern state border.

properties.label: East Anglia
properties.info: East Anglia was under Danish rule after the Viking conquest in the ninth century. The exact boundaries and rulers around 900 are uncertain; modern counties are used as broad proxies.

properties.label: Northumbria
properties.info: York and much of Northumbria were controlled by Norse rulers around 900. The exact extent shifted and is approximated here with modern counties in northern England.

962.note: Europe in 962: Otto I is crowned emperor in Rome, East Francia becomes the Holy Roman Empire, and his power extends into Italy. Lotharingia is incorporated into the imperial sphere, while Normandy, England, Hungary, Croatia and the Kingdom of Arles are shown in their later-tenth-century forms. Borders remain approximate and use modern administrative regions as map proxies.

properties.info: Lothair ruled West Francia from 954 to 986. The kingdom remained distinct from Otto I's East Frankish empire, although the two rulers competed for influence. Modern French regions are approximate map units.

properties.label: Holy Roman Empire
properties.info: On 2 February 962, Pope John XII crowned Otto I emperor in Rome. The imperial title revived the western emperorship and connected the East Frankish kingdom, Italy and the papacy, although authority remained negotiated with powerful princes and cities. Modern regions are broad map proxies.

Otto I took control of the Kingdom of Italy after defeating Berengar II and was crowned emperor in Rome in 962. Italy remained a distinct kingdom within Otto's imperial realm, not a single administratively uniform state. Southern principalities and Byzantine territories are shown separately.

properties.label: Arles
properties.info: The Kingdom of Arles, also called the Kingdom of Burgundy, united Upper and Lower Burgundy in 933 under Rudolf II and was ruled by Conrad the Peaceful in 962. This layer combines the inherited Swiss and southeastern French map proxies; the borders are not historical administrative lines.

Lower Burgundy and Upper Burgundy had been united in the Kingdom of Arles since 933. This layer is grouped with the Arles label and represents its southeastern French territories using modern regions as approximate proxies.

properties.label: Moravia
properties.info: Great Moravia disintegrated in the early tenth century after Magyar invasions. By 962, Moravia was under local and Bohemian influence, while Slovakia had entered the Hungarian sphere. This approximate layer shows only the Moravian regions of today's Czech Republic.

properties.label: Hungary
properties.info: The Magyars had settled in the Carpathian Basin by the late ninth century. In 962 the polity was a principality under Taksony; the later Kingdom of Hungary had not yet been founded. Modern Hungary, Slovakia, parts of Transylvania and the Danube frontier are rough proxies.

properties.label: Croatia
properties.info: Croatia had become a kingdom in the early tenth century, traditionally associated with Tomislav's reign. In 962, Michael Krešimir II ruled; modern Croatian regions provide only a rough approximation.
Peter I ruled Bulgaria from 927 to 969. His reign began with a long peace with Byzantium, although the empire retained influence across much of the Balkans. The map's frontier is approximate.

Romanos II ruled the Byzantine Empire from 959 to 963. Byzantium retained Greece, much of Anatolia and parts of southern Italy; frontiers with Bulgaria and local Balkan rulers remained fluid. Modern regions are approximate map units.

properties.label: Córdoba
properties.info: Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed the Caliphate of Córdoba in 929. His son al-Hakam II ruled from 961 to 976. Its Iberian extent is approximated using modern administrative regions.

properties.label: León
properties.info: The Kingdom of León emerged from the Asturian realm in 910. Sancho I ruled in 962; the northern Iberian map area is an approximate proxy for the kingdom and its frontier.
García Sánchez I ruled Pamplona from 925 to 970. The kingdom occupied a shifting Pyrenean sphere; modern provinces are only approximate references.
Borrell II ruled Barcelona from 947 to 992. The county remained a frontier polity with growing autonomy; modern provinces are map proxies, not historical borders.

properties.label: England
properties.info: Edgar ruled the English kingdom from 959 to 975. Wessex, Mercia and the former Danelaw territories were brought under one king by the mid-tenth century; the modern county polygons shown here are approximate.
Harald Bluetooth consolidated Danish royal power in the later tenth century and was ruling by around 962. The map uses modern Danish regions as broad proxies.

properties.label: Norway
properties.info: Harald Greycloak was king of Norway from about 961 to 970. Royal authority remained uneven and the chronology is debated; the map's southern core is a rough proxy, not a precise frontier.

properties.label: Iceland
properties.info: Iceland had been settled by Norse communities and organized as a commonwealth by the establishment of the Althing around 930. Local chieftains and assemblies shared political authority; modern regions are geographic references only.

properties.label: Normandy
properties.info: The Duchy of Normandy was established after the 911 settlement between Rollo and Charles the Simple. Richard I ruled from 942. The map combines modern Norman departments and nearby Channel Islands as broad proxies.

properties.leader: Local Serbian rulers after Časlav; authority uncertain
properties.info: After the death of Časlav around 960, Serbian lands fragmented and came under competing Byzantine, Bulgarian and Hungarian influence. The broad modern-region grouping is not a claim of a unified or stable 962 state.
Boleslaus I ruled Bohemia from 935 to 972 and expanded Přemyslid power. Bohemia was increasingly connected to Otto I's imperial sphere; modern provinces are approximate map units.
Sviatoslav I ruled the Rus' polity from 945 to 972. The realm remained a network of princely centers rather than a uniformly governed state; modern regions are broad proxies.
Burchard III was duke of Swabia from 954 to 973 within Otto I's imperial realm. Modern Swiss cantons are used as approximate map references.
Indulf ruled Alba from 954 until his death in 962. The existing Scottish mainland grouping is a broad proxy; Norse influence and royal control varied by region.

John XII was pope from 955 to 964 and crowned Otto I emperor in Rome in 962. Papal territory remained politically distinct from the imperial kingdom of Italy; the map uses modern regions as approximate proxies.
Landulf III and his son Pandulf I held power in Benevento in the 960s. Southern Italian principalities remained independent of Otto I's northern Italian kingdom; modern provinces are broad proxies.
Pandulf I Ironhead became prince of Capua in 961 and built a powerful position in southern Italy. Modern provinces are approximate map references.
Gisulf I ruled Salerno from 946 to 977. The principality remained a distinct southern Italian state; modern regions are approximate map units.
Sicily was under Muslim Kalbid rule in 962. The exact succession and dating of individual emirs are not fully secure; the island's modern provinces are geographic proxies.
John III ruled the Duchy of Naples in the mid-tenth century. Naples remained a locally governed duchy in the Byzantine sphere; modern provinces are map proxies.

properties.label: Ikhshidid Emirate
properties.info: Egypt and much of Syria and Palestine were ruled by the Ikhshidid regime in 962, with Abu al-Misk Kafur as the effective ruler. The Fatimids conquered Egypt only in 969. This inherited eastern Mediterranean area is a broad approximation.
The Hamdanid ruler Sayf al-Dawla governed Aleppo from 945 to 967. His emirate was a major regional power between Byzantium and the Abbasid and Fatimid spheres.

properties.label: Ifriqiya
properties.info: The Zirid dynasty had not yet been established in 962; Zirid rule in Ifriqiya began in 972. The region remained under Fatimid authority, represented here with broad modern-region proxies.
Polotsk was an early East Slavic center, but a securely documented independent principality and its tenth-century rulers are uncertain. The modern Belarusian region is only a geographic proxy.
Leon III ruled the Kingdom of Abkhazia from about 957 to 967. Its influence extended across western Georgia; modern regions are approximate proxies.
Gurgen II ruled Tao from 958 to 1008, while the wider Bagratid family competed for influence across Georgian principalities. Modern regions are broad map references.
Kvirike II ruled Kakheti from about 929 to 976. The kingdom was one of several Georgian polities; modern regions are approximate map units.

properties.leader: Muhammad ibn Shaddad and Muhammad ibn Ahmad (Shirvanshah)
properties.info: The Shaddadids emerged in Arran in the mid-tenth century, alongside the Shirvanshah dynasty. This layer represents neighboring local dynasties rather than a unified realm; the boundaries are approximate.

properties.leader: Ashot III of Armenia and regional princes
properties.info: Ashot III ruled the Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia from 952 to 977, alongside other Armenian kingdoms and principalities. This combined layer is a simplification of multiple neighboring dynasties.

properties.label: Upper Mesopotamia
properties.info: The Marwanid dynasty did not rise to power until the later tenth century. In 962, upper Mesopotamia was governed by several local dynasties; this layer is a deliberately broad regional proxy.
Duklja's rulers and political alignment in 962 are poorly documented. The modern Montenegrin regions shown are only broad geographic proxies.
Bosnia was a small inland region whose rulers and relationship to neighboring powers are poorly documented in 962. The modern-area grouping is a cartographic approximation.

properties.leader: Norse earls and local rulers; names uncertain
properties.info: Orkney and the Northern Isles formed part of the Norse world, but the later well-documented earls should not be projected back onto 962. Modern island polygons are geographic proxies.

properties.label: Deheubarth
properties.info: Seisyllwg had been incorporated into the kingdom of Deheubarth by the tenth century. Owain ap Hywel ruled Deheubarth around 962; the map's modern Welsh regions are approximate.
Iago ab Idwal ruled Gwynedd from about 950 to 979. Welsh authority and borders were shaped by dynastic rivalry and English pressure; modern regions are only broad proxies.
Powys remained a Welsh political region, though its rulers and degree of independence around 962 are uncertain. Modern areas are approximate map references.
Morgan ab Owain ruled Morgannwg in the mid-tenth century. Its precise extent is uncertain; modern Welsh areas are used only as a broad proxy.
The Ulaid and neighboring dynasties competed for power in northeast Ireland. The modern Northern Ireland grouping is not a precise historical kingdom boundary.
Connacht was ruled by competing regional dynasties in the tenth century. The mapped area is a broad modern-region approximation rather than a surveyed frontier.
Leinster was divided among local dynasties and contested with the Uí Néill overkings. Modern regions provide only a broad map proxy.
Mathgamain mac Cennétig was an important Munster ruler in the later tenth century. The later ascendancy of Brian Boru should not be projected back to 962; modern regions are approximate.

1066.note: Late-1066 draft: existing provinces are regrouped for the British Isles, Iberia, Italy, the Balkans, eastern Europe, the Caucasus, North Africa and Arabia. Abkhazia and central Kartli are shown as the Kingdom of Georgia; the former Tao area is represented in the Byzantine sphere. The Seljuk sphere is shown across Iran and Iraq; Baghdad is marked as the Abbasid caliphal seat, not a separate territorial state. The Hejaz, eastern Arabia and interior tribal regions are distinguished using modern Saudi regions as broad proxies. Boundaries are approximate; other areas inherit year 1000.

properties.info: In late 1066, Philip I was king of the Franks. This layer shows the broad Kingdom of France using existing modern province areas, not direct royal administration: powerful dukes and counts governed much of the kingdom with substantial autonomy. Normandy and the former Kingdom of Burgundy are shown separately, and Roussillon is mapped as a separate county. These are cartographic approximations, not medieval borders.

properties.label: Taifa of Córdoba
properties.info: After the Caliphate of Córdoba dissolved in 1031, Córdoba became one of several independent taifa states. This layer uses the existing Córdoba province as a rough core. Ceuta and Melilla remain as uncertain southern outliers inherited from the old map; their control is not asserted as a precise 1066 frontier.

properties.label: Kingdom of León
properties.info: After Ferdinand I's death in 1065, his territories were divided among his sons. Alfonso VI received León. This grouping uses existing modern provinces as a broad proxy; the partition and its borders were political and contested, not equivalent to modern provincial boundaries.
Sancho IV Garcés ruled Pamplona/Navarre in 1066. The layer retains the existing province areas as an approximation and does not imply that their modern borders were medieval frontiers.

Ramon Berenguer I ruled the County of Barcelona in 1066. The layer retains its existing province areas as a cartographic proxy; neighboring Catalan counties, including Roussillon, had their own rulers.

Pope Alexander II led the Papal States in 1066. The existing central Italian provinces show a broad papal sphere; local powers and the exact reach of papal administration varied, so these modern provinces are not medieval borders.

Benevento remained a Lombard principality under Pandulf III and his son Landulf VI in 1066. The existing province areas are a rough proxy for a small polity whose authority was increasingly constrained by the Normans and the papacy.

Richard I, a Norman, had taken Capua in 1058. The existing province areas retain the map's broad outline; Norman and Lombard authority in southern Italy remained contested and did not follow modern provincial borders.
Gisulf II ruled Salerno in 1066. The existing province areas are a simplified proxy; the principality was under growing pressure from the Normans and neighboring Lombard powers.

properties.leader: Local Muslim qāʾids; no unified emir
properties.label: Muslim Sicily
properties.info: By 1066 the old Kalbid emirate had fragmented into rival Muslim-led local polities. The map keeps the existing Sicilian province group as a simplified island-wide Muslim sphere; it does not imply one unified ruler or exact control. Norman conquest was underway but was not completed until 1091.

Sergius V ruled the Duchy of Naples in 1066. Naples remained a distinct local duchy amid the competing Norman, Lombard and Byzantine powers of southern Italy; the existing province is a cartographic proxy.

properties.label: Byzantium
properties.info: In 1066 Constantine X Doukas ruled the Byzantine Empire. Bulgaria had been conquered by Basil II in 1018 and was within the Byzantine imperial system, though local resistance and frontier autonomy persisted; the map therefore shows the existing Bulgarian and Macedonian province units in the Byzantine sphere. The Samtskhe-Javakheti unit approximates Byzantine-held Tao, though authority in the Georgian borderlands was contested. Byzantine authority in the Balkans and southern Italy varied, and modern provinces are only broad proxies, not precise borders. Norman expansion in Apulia and Calabria is shown separately.

Peter Krešimir IV ruled Croatia in 1066, when the kingdom was a major power along the Adriatic. The existing Croatian province grouping is retained as an approximate map proxy; Dalmatian cities and frontier authority had layered or changing status.

Mihailo I Vojislavljević ruled Duklja in 1066. The existing Montenegro province areas remain a broad geographic proxy; Duklja's influence and relationship with Byzantium varied, and these are not exact medieval borders.

properties.leader: Local elites; ruler and status uncertain
properties.info: Bosnia is shown as a regional polity using the same existing province areas. Its political status and local rulers in 1066 are uncertain, and influence from neighboring Duklja, Croatia and Byzantium should not be mistaken for a fixed modern-style border.
Solomon was king of Hungary in 1066. The existing province areas are retained as a broad proxy for the kingdom and its frontier influence; modern administrative boundaries are not historical borders.

Sardinia's local giudicati were developing into distinct autonomous powers by the eleventh century. This layer keeps the existing island province group as a simplified illustration of local rule, not as a single unified polity or exact boundary.

Sweyn II ruled Denmark in 1066. The mapped Danish core includes the existing province areas in Jutland and the islands, with Scania, Halland and Blekinge shown within the Danish sphere. These are modern administrative proxies, not exact medieval borders.

properties.leader: Olaf Kyrre and Magnus II Haraldsson
properties.info: After Harald Hardrada's death in 1066, his sons Olaf Kyrre and Magnus II ruled Norway jointly until 1069. The map retains the existing southern and central Norwegian province proxies; it does not imply uniform royal control over every northern or frontier region.

The mapped Swedish heartland uses the same existing provincial areas as the year-1000 layer. Royal authority was uneven and the succession after Stenkil's death in 1066 is uncertain; these modern regions are approximate, not firm historical borders.

In 1066 Henry IV, King of the Romans, had begun his personal rule after years of regency. This approximate imperial sphere includes the former Kingdom of Burgundy, incorporated into the Empire under Conrad II in 1032. The Empire remained a patchwork of realms, duchies and lordships, not a uniformly administered state; modern provinces do not reproduce its medieval borders.

properties.leader: Bolesław II the Bold (Duke of Poland)
properties.info: Bolesław II ruled Poland as duke in 1066; he was crowned king in 1076. This layer keeps the existing Polish province grouping but removes the Moravian areas previously shown as Polish around 1000. Modern regional boundaries are only approximate proxies for medieval control.

Vratislaus II ruled Bohemia as duke from 1061; he did not receive the royal title until 1085. The existing Bohemian core is retained, and Moravia's appanage duchies are grouped with Bohemia for simplicity. This is a broad depiction of Přemyslid rule, not a claim that Bohemia was directly administered as one unit.

properties.leader: Iziaslav I Yaroslavich (Grand Prince of Kyiv)
properties.info: Iziaslav I was Grand Prince of Kyiv in 1066. Kievan Rus' was a network of princely territories rather than a centralized state; Polotsk is shown separately under Vseslav. The map retains the existing broad regional outline, which does not represent exact princely frontiers.

Vseslav Bryachislavich ruled Polotsk in 1066. Polotsk was a distinct and often rival princely center within the wider world of the Rus' lands; the existing Vitebsk province is only a small modern map proxy for its territory.

Estonia remained divided among local communities and strongholds rather than united as one kingdom in 1066. The existing modern administrative regions are used only as a broad geographic proxy; political authority and frontiers were local and fluid.

properties.leader: Curonian, Latgalian, Semigallian and Selonian local leaders
properties.info: The eastern Baltic remained politically fragmented in 1066, with Curonian, Latgalian, Semigallian and Selonian communities and local leaders. The existing Latvia regions are a broad map proxy and do not imply a single unified realm or precise borders.
Lithuanian communities were not yet represented here as one centralized kingdom in 1066. The existing modern Lithuanian regions are a geographic proxy only; local authority and boundaries were fluid.

Old Prussian communities remained organized among local groups in 1066, without a single ruler for the whole region. The existing Kaliningrad and Warmian-Masurian units are only rough map references, not exact tribal borders.
Yotvingian communities occupied a changing frontier zone between Baltic and East Slavic powers. The existing Podlaskie province is only a broad geographic proxy, not a precise 1066 boundary.

Finnic communities in present-day southern and central Finland remained locally organized in 1066. The existing modern province units are geographic proxies and should not be read as fixed medieval borders.

Karelian communities occupied a frontier between the Baltic world and the lands of Novgorod and other Rus' princes. The existing North and South Karelia and Karelia map units are only rough geographic references.

Northern Finnic and Samoyedic communities remained outside a single securely defined kingdom in 1066. The existing large modern regions are broad frontier proxies, not claims of uniform rule or exact borders.

properties.leader: Sámi communities and local northern leaders
properties.info: Sámi communities and northern frontier groups maintained local forms of authority in 1066. The existing modern northern provinces are geographic references only; they do not imply fixed borders or uniform rule.

Heveller and Sprewaner communities remained locally ruled in 1066. This layer keeps the existing Berlin and Brandenburg map units as a rough geographic proxy, not as a unified state with surveyed borders.

The Obotrite ruler Gottschalk was killed in an uprising in 1066, after which Kruto took power. The existing Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania unit remains a broad regional proxy and does not represent exact tribal or political borders.
Rudolf of Rheinfelden was Duke of Swabia in 1066. This layer retains the existing Swiss-region map units as an approximate depiction of the duchy's southern sphere, not exact medieval boundaries.

Aghsartan I ruled Kakheti in 1066. The eastern Georgian kingdom retained its own rulers and resisted full integration into Bagrat IV's Kingdom of Georgia. The existing Kakheti map unit is only a modern geographic proxy.

properties.leader: Abu al-Hayja ibn Ja'far (Ja'farid; identification tentative)
properties.info: Tbilisi remained under a Muslim emirate in 1066, separate from the neighboring Georgian kingdoms. Numismatic evidence points to a Ja'farid ruler, possibly Abu al-Hayja ibn Ja'far, but identification for this exact year is uncertain. The existing Tbilisi region is a rough map proxy.

properties.leader: Abu'l-Aswar Shavur I (Arran) and Fariburz I (Shirvan)
properties.info: The existing area combines distinct powers: the Shaddadids under Abu'l-Aswar Shavur I around Ganja and the Shirvanshahs under Fariburz I farther east. Their borders and relative power shifted, and the available map geometry cannot distinguish them reliably.

properties.leader: Kiurike II and other Armenian princes; no single ruler
properties.info: The Bagratid Kingdom of Ani had been annexed by Byzantium in 1045. Armenian principalities nevertheless survived, including Tashir-Dzoraget (Lori) under Kiurike II. This layer keeps a broad composite of Armenian regions and must not be read as an independent Kingdom of Ani or a single unified Armenian state; modern provinces are only rough proxies.

Nizam al-Dawla Nasr ruled the Marwanid emirate from 1061 to 1079. The state centered on Amid and Mayyafariqin faced growing Seljuk pressure; its mapped modern provinces are only a rough approximation of shifting control.

Durgulel ruled Alania during the 1060s, when the Christian Alanian kingdom was an important power in the North Caucasus and maintained close ties with Byzantium and Georgia. The existing North Ossetia, Kabardino-Balkaria and Karachay-Cherkess map units remain broad geographic proxies; Alania's historical extent did not follow these modern boundaries.

properties.leader: Local rulers and communities; no single ruler
properties.info: Outside Alania, the North Caucasus contained diverse local communities and political groupings, including Circassian, Vainakh and Dagestani populations, with authority varying by valley and locality. This layer is not a unified state, and its existing modern-region filters are only broad geographic markers, not fixed 1066 borders.

Al-Mustansir Billah was Fatimid caliph in 1066, but political and military crises weakened central authority. The existing layer shows Egypt and a broad, uneven sphere in the Levant, not uniform Fatimid administration; local powers and Byzantine rivalry shaped control.

Mahmud ibn Nasr ruled the Mirdasid emirate of Aleppo in 1066. The existing Aleppo governorate is a rough regional proxy, not the emirate's exact frontier; it navigated pressure from the Fatimids, Byzantines and Seljuks.

Tamim ibn al-Mu'izz ruled the Zirid dynasty from 1062. After the Hilalian invasion and the loss of Kairouan, effective Zirid power contracted toward coastal centers, especially Mahdia. The selected Tunisian coastal provinces are broad modern proxies; the retained eastern Algerian and Tripolitan filters are less certain and should not be read as uniform Zirid control.

The western and central Maghreb remained politically fragmented in 1066. Hammadid, Maghrawa, Zenata and other local powers held shifting areas; this broad layer also includes eastern Algerian provinces where Zirid authority was weakened after the Hilalian incursions. It is a composite map proxy, not a unified realm or exact border.

The Sahara and its margins consisted of local Amazigh, Sanhaja and Tuareg communities and trade networks rather than one state. The Almoravid movement was emerging among Sanhaja groups in the eleventh century. Modern administrative regions remain rough geographic markers only.

properties.leader: Byzantine Cherson and local steppe powers
properties.info: In 1066 Byzantine authority remained centered on Cherson in southwestern Crimea, while much of the peninsula and steppe hinterland was outside firm imperial control. Pecheneg and increasingly Cuman pressure shaped the region. The existing whole-peninsula map units are only a broad frontier proxy, not a single realm's precise territory.

properties.leader: Pecheneg groups and other steppe powers
properties.info: The lower Danube and Black Sea steppe remained a shifting frontier in 1066. Pecheneg groups were under pressure from neighboring powers and the rising Cumans; the existing regions represent a broad zone of movement and influence, not a centralized state or precise border.

Volga Bulgaria remained a major trading polity around the middle Volga and Kama rivers in 1066. The existing Tatarstan and Chuvashia map units are only a rough reference and do not reproduce the state's historical borders.

Beyond Volga Bulgaria's core, the Volga-Ural zone was home to diverse Finnic and Turkic communities, including Bashkir groups, with local authority and tributary ties that shifted over time. The added southern and central Ural units are especially broad modern map proxies; this layer represents a frontier zone, not one unified state or precise border.

Iceland remained a self-governing commonwealth in 1066, without a king. Political authority rested with local chieftains and institutions including the Althing. The existing island regions are only geographic map references.

By 1066 the Faroes were under Norwegian overlordship, traditionally associated with Leivur Øssursson accepting the islands as a fief from Magnus the Good after 1035. Local authority remained important, and the existing island polygon is a map reference rather than a precise statement of royal administration.

Gotland retained strong local institutions and a distinct trading community in 1066. Its relationship with the Swedish kings was developing and should not be read as identical to direct royal administration. The existing island province is retained as a geographic proxy.

The existing island provinces show a broad Norse sphere around Orkney and Shetland, with Norse influence in the Hebrides. In 1066 Orkney was ruled jointly by the earls Paul and Erlend; island authority and overlordship were layered and do not form a precise modern-style border.

properties.label: Norman England
properties.info: In this late-1066 snapshot, William, Duke of Normandy, is shown as King of England after his coronation at Westminster on 25 December, following the Battle of Hastings on 14 October. England and Normandy were separate political entities under one ruler, not a single formally merged country. This layer retains the year-1000 English province proxies and does not claim that William had secured every part of England by year-end.

properties.leader: William I (William the Conqueror), also King of England
properties.info: In late 1066, William ruled Normandy as duke and England as king. They were separate political entities under one ruler, not one formally merged country. Their shared ruler linked them within the Anglo-Norman realm, but their institutions and status remained distinct; they did not later become a single country. The existing provinces are modern map proxies, not exact medieval borders.

Malcolm III had ruled Alba since 1058. This layer retains the modern Scottish mainland as a broad cartographic proxy; royal authority, especially in the north and west, was uneven, and the exact southern frontier was not a fixed modern border. Norse island territories are shown separately.

properties.label: Gwynedd and Powys
properties.info: After Gruffudd ap Llywelyn's death in 1063, Bleddyn and Rhiwallon ap Cynfyn succeeded to the former domains of Gwynedd and Powys under Edward the Confessor's overlordship. These existing Welsh provinces are grouped together as a broad territorial proxy, not a surveyed frontier.

Maredudd ab Owain ab Edwin restored his family's rule in Deheubarth after Gruffudd ap Llywelyn's death in 1063. This area uses modern Welsh administrative regions as a broad proxy; historical control and borders were not equivalent to today's county lines.

This broad western part of the former Morgannwg grouping is shown separately from Caradog ap Gruffydd's documented power base in Gwynllwg and Upper Gwent. Existing modern Welsh provinces are only approximate proxies for fluid 11th-century lordships.

properties.leader: Northern Irish dynasties; authority was divided
properties.info: Northern Ireland was not a single unified territory under one ruler in 1066. Cenél nEógain, Cenél Conaill, Ulaid and other dynasties held competing regional power. The modern counties shown here are only a broad geographic reference, not a reconstruction of their boundaries.

Áed in Gai Bernaig was king of Connacht in 1066. Irish kingship involved overlapping claims and shifting influence; the modern counties shown here are a broad provincial proxy, not a precise political frontier.

Diarmait mac Máel na mBó ruled Leinster and held Dublin from 1052, installing his son Murchad as king there. The layer's modern county boundaries are approximate; Norse Dublin remained a distinct urban and maritime centre within Diarmait's sphere.

Toirdelbach Ua Briain succeeded to Munster's kingship in 1063–1064 after Donnchad mac Briain's exile. His influence extended beyond Munster at times, but Ireland had no settled, universally accepted central kingship. Modern counties here are only a broad provincial proxy.

properties.label: Mecca
properties.info: Abu Hashim Muhammad ibn Ja'far became emir (sharif) of Mecca in 1063. Mecca had strong local Hashimite leadership and remained within the wider Fatimid-Sulayhid sphere of influence; allegiance and practical control were contested and could shift. The modern Makkah Region is only a geographic proxy, not the sharifate's exact territory.

properties.leader: Local Hasanid sharifs; individual ruler uncertain
properties.label: Medina
properties.info: Medina had its own local sharifian leadership in the eleventh century and was not necessarily governed by the emir of Mecca. The individual ruler in 1066 is uncertain; the existing Al Madinah Region is only a broad geographic reference.

properties.leader: Collective Qarmatian leadership; individual ruler uncertain
properties.label: Qarmatian east
properties.info: In 1066 the weakened Qarmatian state still held al-Hasa and parts of the eastern Arabian coast, including the region historically called Bahrain. Its collective leadership was divided, and the state fell to the Uyunids around 1076-1077. The modern Eastern Region and Bahrain polygons are broad geographic proxies, not exact borders.

properties.leader: Local Arab tribal leaders; no single ruler
properties.label: Arabian tribal lands
properties.info: Much of the Arabian interior and frontier in 1066 was organized through local tribes, oasis communities and shifting alliances rather than a single kingdom. The southern highlands also interacted with the Sulayhid power in Yemen. These remaining modern Saudi regions are broad map markers only and should not be read as one unified state or fixed border.

properties.label: Seljuk Sultanate
properties.info: Alp Arslan ruled the Great Seljuk Sultanate from 1063 to 1072. In 1066 Seljuk political and military power extended across Iran and Iraq, although local dynasties and provincial authority varied. The modern map units are broad territorial proxies, not precise borders; Baghdad is separately marked only as the Abbasid caliphal seat, not as an independent state.

properties.label: Baghdad (Abbasid Caliph)
properties.info: Caliph al-Qa'im remained the Abbasid caliph in 1066. Baghdad is highlighted as the caliphal seat and center of religious legitimacy, not as an independent territorial state: effective military and political power in Iraq rested with the Seljuk sultanate.

properties.leader: Hilalian groups and local authorities; no single ruler
properties.label: Ifriqiyan hinterland
properties.info: After the Hilalian incursions and the loss of Kairouan, much of inland Ifriqiya lay beyond effective Zirid rule and was influenced by migrating Bedouin groups and local authorities. These existing Tunisian governorates are a deliberately broad proxy for a fragmented hinterland, not a single Hilalian state or fixed frontier.

properties.label: Georgia
properties.info: Bagrat IV ruled the Kingdom of Georgia in 1066. This layer combines the existing Abkhazian and central Kartlian map units after the political unification of 1008. Kakheti and the Muslim emirate of Tbilisi remained separate; Tao had been ceded to Byzantium earlier in the century, so these modern regions are only a broad geographic approximation.

Meath (Mide) was a distinct Irish kingdom in 1066 under Conchobar Ua Máel Sechlainn. This broad outline uses the existing county polygons for Meath and neighbouring areas; it is an approximation, not a precise medieval frontier.
properties.label: Meath

properties.info: Dublin was a distinct Hiberno-Norse kingdom. In 1066 Murchad mac Diarmata, son of Diarmait mac Máel na mBó of Leinster, ruled Dublin and the Isle of Man under his father's wider power. The mapped outline uses existing Dublin-area county polygons as a geographic proxy.
properties.label: Dublin

properties.info: Caradog ap Gruffydd's family power base lay in Gwynllwg and Upper Gwent. These existing modern Welsh provinces are used as a broad proxy for that area; they do not reproduce an exact 11th-century boundary.
properties.label: Gwent
Roussillon
properties.info: In 1066 Roussillon was a separate county ruled by Gausfred II. The existing Pyrénées-Orientales province is used as a rough map proxy; it is not an exact historical border.

properties.label: Galicia
properties.info: Ferdinand I's division created a separate Kingdom of Galicia for García II after 1065. The four existing Galician province areas are a broad proxy, not exact medieval borders.

properties.label: Castile
properties.info: After Ferdinand I's death in 1065, Sancho II received Castile. This grouping uses existing modern province areas as a broad proxy; the frontier with León was contested and did not follow modern provincial borders.

properties.label: Seville
properties.info: The Abbadid taifa of Seville was an independent Muslim kingdom in 1066. The mapped southern Spanish and Portuguese areas are approximate provincial proxies; taifa boundaries and overlordship changed over time.

properties.label: Badajoz
properties.info: The Aftasid taifa of Badajoz was a major power in western Iberia. These existing Portuguese and Spanish province areas give only a broad regional outline; control near Seville and León was contested and changed rapidly.

properties.label: Toledo
properties.info: Yahya ibn Isma'il al-Ma'mun ruled the taifa of Toledo in 1066. Existing central Iberian province areas are used as approximate proxies, not exact borders.

properties.label: Granada
properties.info: The Zirid taifa of Granada was ruled by Badis ibn Habus in 1066. The mapped Andalusi province areas are broad proxies; modern administrative boundaries are not historical frontiers.

properties.label: Murcia
properties.info: The taifa of Murcia emerged as an independent power in the mid-11th century under the Banu Tahir. These existing southeastern province areas are approximate; local control and borders were fluid.

properties.label: Valencia
properties.info: Valencia was an independent taifa in 1066. This regional grouping follows existing modern province areas as a broad proxy, not a precise historical border.

properties.label: Zaragoza
properties.info: The Hudid taifa of Zaragoza, ruled by Ahmad al-Muqtadir in 1066, fills the previously unassigned Zaragoza province. Huesca and Teruel are included as broad existing-province proxies; actual frontier control was contested.

properties.realm: Taifa of Denia and the Balearics
properties.label: Denia and the Balearics
properties.info: Denia and the Balearic Islands were linked under the taifa ruled by Ali ibn Mujahid in the mid-11th century. The existing Balearic province is an approximate map unit, not a precise historical boundary.

properties.label: Norman holdings
properties.info: Robert Guiscard was recognized as duke of Apulia and Calabria in 1059, while Byzantine strongholds and contested areas remained. These existing province units are a deliberately rough indication of Norman expansion by 1066, not a precise frontier or claim that every part of southern Italy was under uniform Norman control.

properties.label: Serbian lands
properties.info: The Serbian lands were divided among local rulers, with Byzantine influence and overlordship varying over time. Existing Serbian and Kosovo province units provide only a broad regional picture and should not be read as one centralized kingdom with fixed borders.

1100.note: Late-1100 snapshot. The map reuses the existing province polygons and the 1066 grouping as its base, changing control where the existing map units allow it. Henry I had taken the English throne, while Robert Curthose remained duke of Normandy. Most Iberian taifas had been absorbed by the Almoravids; León and Castile were united under Alfonso VI, and Portugal was an autonomous county. Norman rule had replaced Muslim rule in Sicily. The First Crusade established the counties of Edessa and Antioch and the Kingdom of Jerusalem; Ascalon remained Fatimid. Anatolian and other frontiers are broad modern-region approximations, not exact medieval borders. Unchanged regions retain their 1066 grouping and descriptive metadata.

properties.info: Philip I remained king of the Franks in 1100. This layer keeps the broad royal-domain proxy from the prior snapshot; powerful dukes and counts held much of the kingdom with substantial autonomy.

properties.label: England
properties.info: Henry I became king after William II's death in August 1100. England was ruled by the Norman dynasty, but its population and language were still predominantly English; this map does not represent a newly created Norman culture. The existing English province polygons are approximate map units.

properties.label: Normandy
properties.info: Robert Curthose ruled Normandy as a distinct duchy, separate from his brother Henry I's kingdom of England; the personal union shown in 1066 had ended. Normandy was nominally a fief of the French king, but remained under its own duke rather than being directly ruled from Paris. The existing provinces are broad map proxies.

Edgar ruled Alba from 1097 to 1107. The modern Scottish mainland remains a broad map proxy; royal authority, especially in the north and west, was uneven, and Norse island territories are shown separately.

properties.label: León-Castile
properties.info: Alfonso VI ruled León and Castile together and held Toledo, taken in 1085. The existing provincial units combine the inherited León, Castile, Galicia and Toledo groupings; they are approximate modern map proxies, not exact medieval borders.

properties.leader: Pedro I of Aragón and Pamplona
properties.info: Pedro I ruled Aragón and Pamplona in 1100. The existing Navarre grouping is retained as an approximate regional outline.
Ramon Berenguer III ruled Barcelona from 1086. The existing province grouping is retained as a broad cartographic proxy.
Giselbert II ruled Roussillon around 1100. The existing Pyrénées-Orientales province is a rough map proxy, not an exact historical border.
Pope Paschal II led the Papal States in 1100. The existing central Italian map units are broad proxies for papal lands and do not reproduce medieval boundaries.

properties.label: Papal Benevento
properties.info: Benevento had returned to papal control in 1078. Its existing province unit is retained as a separate enclave proxy within the broader papal sphere.
Richard II ruled the Norman principality of Capua in 1100. The existing map units are approximate and do not imply exact medieval borders.

properties.label: Norman Sicily
properties.info: The Norman conquest of Sicily was completed in 1091. Roger I ruled the county in 1100; the existing Sicilian and Maltese map units are broad proxies, not exact boundaries.
Sergius VI ruled Naples in 1100. The duchy remained distinct amid Norman expansion in southern Italy; its existing province is only a map proxy.

properties.label: Byzantium
properties.info: Alexios I Komnenos ruled Byzantium in 1100. After the First Crusade, imperial authority had recovered much of the western Anatolian coast, while the central plateau was held by Turkish powers. The existing modern provinces are broad proxies; Balkan and other inherited areas remain approximate.

properties.leader: Croatian succession disputed; Hungarian influence expanding
properties.info: After Petar Svačić's defeat and death in 1097, Croatia's succession and control were contested as Coloman of Hungary strengthened his claim. Coloman's coronation as king of Croatia is conventionally dated to 1102, so this 1100 snapshot does not treat Croatia as already formally united with Hungary. The existing provincial outline is only an approximate map proxy.
Coloman ruled Hungary in 1100. The existing Hungarian province grouping is retained as an approximate map proxy.

Eric I ruled Denmark from 1095 to 1103. The Danish core and islands are shown using broad modern proxies. The separate modern Schleswig-Holstein polygon is assigned to the imperial layer for map purposes, but around 1100 Schleswig north of the Eider belonged to the Danish sphere while Holstein to the south lay within Saxony and the Empire; this map unit cannot show that division.
Magnus III ruled Norway in 1100. The existing southern and central province proxies do not imply uniform royal control over every northern or frontier region.
Inge the Elder was king in much of Sweden around 1100, though succession and regional authority remained contested. The existing provinces are approximate map references.

Henry IV remained Holy Roman Emperor in 1100. The inherited imperial outline represents a patchwork of duchies and lordships, not uniform administration or exact borders. The modern Schleswig-Holstein polygon is included here as a coarse proxy for imperial Holstein, but it also contains Schleswig, which remained in the Danish sphere; the modern unit cannot represent the medieval Eider frontier.

Władysław I Herman ruled Poland as duke in 1100. Poland was a Piast-ruled duchy, not a territory of the Holy Roman Empire; political and feudal relations with the emperor did not make it an imperial province. The existing province grouping is retained as a broad map proxy.

Bosnia is shown as a regional polity around 1100, but the surviving evidence does not securely identify its ruler or establish a stable border or overlord. The later, better-documented Bosnian banate should not be projected unchanged onto this date. The existing modern province areas are only a rough geographic proxy.

The Obotrite polity in the Mecklenburg region was ruled by Henry the Obotrite from 1093 to 1127. It was a West Slavic power with shifting relations to Saxon and Danish neighbors, not simply part of Denmark, Poland, or the Holy Roman Empire. The existing Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania unit is a broad geographic proxy, not a precise border.

properties.leader: Local Heveller and Sprewaner rulers; individual rulers uncertain
properties.info: The Heveller around the Havel and Sprewaner around the Spree remained distinct West Slavic communities in the Brandenburg-Berlin region; there was no Brandenburg margraviate yet. The two groups are combined only because the map has coarse modern units, and the layer should not be read as a single unified state or as settled imperial territory.
Frederick I of Hohenstaufen was duke of Swabia from 1079 to 1105. The inherited imperial provinces are only broad proxies for a patchwork of lordships.
Bořivoj II became duke of Bohemia in 1100. The existing Bohemian and Moravian units remain a broad proxy for Přemyslid lands.
Sviatopolk II ruled Kyiv in 1100. Kievan Rus' remained a network of princely territories rather than a centralized state; the inherited outline is not an exact princely frontier.
Constantine Bodin ruled Duklja until 1101. The existing Montenegro-based outline is a broad geographic proxy for a principality with shifting authority.

Al-Musta'li was Fatimid caliph in 1100. The map retains Egypt, the southern coastal district around Ascalon, and the contested Lebanese and Jordanian frontier as broad Fatimid spheres after Jerusalem's capture in 1099. Modern administrative areas are rough proxies, not assertions of uniform control.
Ridwan ibn Tutush ruled Aleppo in 1100. The existing Aleppo governorate is a rough regional proxy; northern Syria was divided among rival local and Turkish powers.

By 1100 the Zirid court was centered on Mahdia and retained coastal centers in Tunisia, while much of the inland region lay beyond effective central control. These modern governorates are broad proxies and do not imply uniform rule.

After the Hilalian incursions and the loss of Kairouan, much of inland Ifriqiya and the eastern Algerian hinterland lay beyond effective Zirid rule and was influenced by migrating Bedouin groups and local authorities. These modern governorates are broad proxies for fragmented and contested power, not a single Hilalian state or fixed frontier.

The Sahara and its margins remained home to diverse Amazigh, Sanhaja and Tuareg communities and trade networks in 1100, outside uniform state control. The existing southern map units are broad geographic markers, not precise borders.

properties.label: Almoravids
properties.info: By 1100 Yusuf ibn Tashfin's Almoravid state controlled Morocco and had absorbed most of the Muslim polities of al-Andalus. The map reuses the former Maghreb and taifa province units; Zaragoza, Valencia, the Balearics and Toledo are kept separate. These modern provinces are broad approximations.
The Marwanid emirate had been absorbed by the Great Seljuk sphere by the late eleventh century; its former mapped provinces are reassigned to successor powers in this snapshot.

David IV ruled Georgia in 1100 and was consolidating royal authority. The existing Georgian regions are retained as approximate map units; Kakheti and Tbilisi remained outside his control at this date.

properties.leader: Local Muslim emir under Seljuk suzerainty; individual ruler uncertain
properties.info: Tbilisi remained under a Muslim emirate and Seljuk overlordship around 1100, outside David IV's Georgian kingdom. The existing Tbilisi region is a rough map proxy.

properties.leader: Manuchihr III (Shirvan); Arran under changing Seljuk and local control
properties.info: Shirvan was ruled by Manuchihr III around 1100, while Arran had come under Seljuk influence after the Shaddadid rulers lost power. The combined existing map units blur these distinct and changing authorities.
Kakheti remained a separate kingdom under Aghsartan II around 1100. Its existing regional unit is an approximate map proxy.

By 1100, Cumans had largely displaced the Pechenegs as the dominant power across much of the Pontic steppe. The existing units represent a shifting frontier, not a centralized state or precise border.

properties.label: Uyunid Emirate
properties.info: The Qarmatian state in al-Hasa had fallen to the Uyunid dynasty around 1076-1077. The existing Eastern Region and Bahrain polygons are broad geographic proxies for Uyunid rule.

Barkiyaruq ruled the Great Seljuk Sultanate in 1100 after the succession struggles following Malik-Shah's death. The Iran, Iraq and non-coastal Syrian map units represent a fragmented Seljuk sphere, including local emirates, not uniform central administration.
Al-Mustazhir became Abbasid caliph in 1094. Baghdad is highlighted as the caliphal seat, not an independent territorial state; effective military power in Iraq remained with the Seljuk sultanate.

properties.label: Valencia under Jimena Díaz
properties.info: After El Cid's death in 1099, his widow Jimena Díaz continued to hold Valencia until 1102. The existing province grouping is a broad proxy for this short-lived Christian rule.
Zaragoza remained an independent taifa under the Hudid dynasty around 1100. Its existing province units are broad proxies; the frontier was contested.

properties.label: Mallorca
properties.info: The Balearics remained under a local taifa around 1100, before their later Almoravid conquest. The existing island polygon is a broad map reference.
Roger Borsa ruled the Norman duchy in 1100. Salerno had been absorbed into Norman rule; existing Italian provinces remain only broad proxies for a fragmented southern Italian landscape.
The Serbian lands remained divided among local rulers, with Byzantine influence and overlordship varying over time. Existing Serbian and Kosovo province units are only a broad regional picture.
Meath remained one of several Irish kingdoms in 1100. Existing counties are a broad geographic proxy, not a precise medieval frontier.

Gruffudd ap Cynan had re-established control in Gwynedd by around 1099 and ruled until 1137. The inherited Gwynedd province grouping is approximate; Powys remains separately mapped, and neither realm was under Norman rule.

After Rhys ap Tewdwr was killed in 1093, Deheubarth fragmented and Norman marcher lords seized parts of south Wales. The inherited counties are a broad proxy for remaining Welsh-held areas, not a firm kingdom-wide boundary.

properties.label: Glamorgan
properties.info: Robert Fitzhamon established Norman control over much of Glamorgan from the 1090s. The inherited modern Welsh provinces are a rough proxy for the marcher lordship; Norman authority did not mean uniform control of every upland area.

properties.realm: Norman Lordships of Gwent and Gwynllwg
properties.label: Norman Gwent
properties.leader: Norman marcher lords; local lordships varied
properties.info: Norman marcher lords had taken control of much of Gwent and Gwynllwg by the late eleventh century. These existing Welsh administrative areas are broad proxies, not exact lordship boundaries.

properties.leader: Ruaidrí na Saide Buide Ua Conchobair
properties.info: Ruaidrí na Saide Buide Ua Conchobair was king of Connacht around 1100. The inherited modern-county grouping is a broad proxy, not a precise frontier.
Donnchad mac Murchada ruled Leinster from 1098 to 1115. The inherited modern-county grouping is approximate; Dublin remained a distinct Hiberno-Norse center.
Muirchertach Ua Briain ruled Munster around 1100 and wielded influence beyond it, amid continuing competition among Irish kings. The mapped counties are a broad proxy.
Mann remained a Norse-Gaelic polity around 1100, though its ruler and the degree of its connection to Dublin and Norway are uncertain. The existing island outline is a map proxy.

Dublin remained a distinct Hiberno-Norse political center in 1100, with its ruler and wider overlordship uncertain. The existing Dublin-area counties are broad proxies; Mann is shown separately, and no English or Norman conquest of Ireland had yet occurred.

properties.label: Portugal
properties.info: The County of Portugal was granted to Henry of Burgundy in 1096 under León-Castile's overlordship. Its broad map outline includes Coimbra and the eastern Portuguese frontier; these modern province units do not imply precise county borders or uniform control.

properties.leader: Banu Khazrun dynasty; individual ruler uncertain
properties.label: Tripolitania
properties.info: Tripoli and its western hinterland were ruled by the locally based Banu Khazrun dynasty around 1100, with shifting relations to Zirid and Fatimid powers. The existing Libyan districts are broad proxies for Tripolitanian authority, not precise borders.

properties.leader: Local Arab and Berber authorities; no single ruler securely known
properties.label: Cyrenaica
properties.info: Cyrenaica had no securely documented single territorial ruler around 1100; local authorities and tribal groups held influence amid changing Fatimid, Zirid and Hilalian connections. These modern coastal districts are only regional proxies.

properties.label: Sultanate of Rum
properties.info: The Sultanate of Rum held much of the central Anatolian plateau in 1100 under Kilij Arslan I. The remaining Turkish province polygons are used as broad proxies; western coastal areas are shown as Byzantine, while northeastern districts are left to the Danishmendid sphere.

properties.label: Danishmendids
properties.info: Danishmendid rulers controlled parts of north-central and northeastern Anatolia around 1100. These existing Turkish provinces are a coarse proxy for a fragmented frontier, not an exact boundary.

properties.leader: Local Turkish emirs and Armenian/Kurdish lords (Saltuqids, Artuqids, Shah-Armens); rulers uncertain
properties.label: Eastern emirates
properties.info: Eastern Anatolia and the upper Tigris lands were not part of Kilij Arslan's sultanate around 1100; they were held by small Turkish emirates and local Armenian, Georgian and Kurdish lords. The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Edessa
properties.info: The County of Edessa was founded during the First Crusade. After Baldwin I became king of Jerusalem in 1100, Baldwin II ruled Edessa. The modern Şanlıurfa province is a broad map proxy.

properties.label: Antioch
properties.info: The Principality of Antioch was founded in 1098. At the end of 1100, Tancred acted as regent while Bohemond I was in captivity; Hatay and neighboring Syrian provinces are only rough geographic proxies.

properties.label: Jerusalem
properties.info: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was established after the city fell to the First Crusade in 1099. Baldwin I became king in 1100. Existing Israeli and Palestinian administrative regions are broad proxies; Fatimid Ascalon remained outside the kingdom.

1200.note: Around-1200 snapshot, reusing the existing province polygons and the 1100 grouping and changing control where the map units allow it. Richard I had died in 1199 and John ruled England and the Angevin lands in France (together the Angevin Empire), including Normandy, until Philip II conquered Normandy in 1204. Iberia was divided among Almohad al-Andalus, Portugal, León, Castile, Navarre and the Crown of Aragon. The Kingdom of Sicily was unified under the child Frederick II, and the Empire was split between Philip of Swabia and Otto IV. Byzantium had lost Bulgaria, Serbia, Hungary's Croatia and Cyprus; the Fourth Crusade was still to come. Saladin's Ayyubids ruled Egypt and most of Syria, Jerusalem was Muslim again, and Georgia under Tamar was at its height. Almohads held the whole Maghreb. All borders are broad modern-region approximations, not medieval frontiers; fragmented regions use blanket proxies.

properties.info: Sverker II became king in 1196 and ruled until 1208, in the long rivalry between the Sverker and Eric dynasties. The existing Swedish provinces are broad proxies; royal control in the north and in Finland was weak.

Cnut VI ruled Denmark from 1182 and imposed Danish overlordship over the Obotrites and Pomeranians from 1185. His brother Valdemar II took Holstein and Lübeck from 1201. The existing Danish provinces are broad proxies; Schleswig-Holstein is not separately split.
Sverre ruled Norway from 1184 until 1202, in a long civil war with the Church and the Baglers. Existing Norwegian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Philip of Swabia and Otto IV (rival kings)
properties.info: After Henry VI's death in 1197 the Empire split between Philip of Swabia and Otto IV of Brunswick, who had papal support from 1201. Northern Italian cities formed the Lombard League and were largely self-governing. The existing provinces are broad proxies for imperial lands, not exact medieval borders.

properties.label: Brandenburg
properties.info: Albert the Bear founded the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1157 on former Heveller land. Otto II ruled it from 1184 as a prince of the Empire. The existing Berlin and Brandenburg polygons are broad proxies.
The Obotrite princes under Henry Borwin I had to recognize Danish overlordship from 1185, while German settlement advanced. The existing Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania polygon is a broad proxy.

Philip II ruled France and had gained Artois, Vermandois and Amiens. Angevin Normandy, Brittany and western France lay outside his direct control until 1204 and later, and the southern regions were largely held by powerful counts. This layer                     is a broad royal-domain proxy and covers more than Philip actually controlled.

properties.leader: Fragmented Piast duchies; seniority contested (Mieszko III the Old and Leszek the White)
properties.info: Since Bolesław III's testament of 1138, Poland was divided among Piast duchies with a contested senior duke. The existing Polish provinces remain a single proxy, but the Piast dukes did not form a unified state.
Innocent III (1198–1216) recovered papal control in central Italy and acted as guardian of the young Frederick of Sicily. The existing central Italian provinces are broad proxies for papal lands.
Benevento remained a papal enclave inside the Kingdom of Sicily; its existing provinces are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Sicily
properties.leader: Frederick II (child king; Pope Innocent III as guardian)
properties.info: Roger II united southern Italy and Sicily as a kingdom in 1130, absorbing Capua, Naples, Salerno and Apulia. After Henry VI and Constance died (1197 and 1198), the child Frederick II was king under papal guardianship while German and local barons contested power. Existing Italian provinces and Malta are broad proxies; the papal enclave of Benevento is shown separately.
Philip of Hohenstaufen was duke of Swabia from 1196 and king of Germany from 1198, in rivalry with Otto IV. The existing Swiss-area provinces are only a rough proxy for the duchy.

properties.label: Bohemia
properties.info: Ottokar I was duke from 1197 and received a royal title from Philip of Swabia in 1198, though the hereditary royal title was confirmed only in 1212. The realm remained within the Empire. Existing Czech provinces are broad proxies.

Emeric succeeded Béla III in 1196 and ruled Hungary and Croatia, with a rival claim from his brother Andrew. The existing provinces for Hungary, Slovakia, Transylvania and Vojvodina are broad proxies, not exact medieval borders.

properties.label: Croatia (Hungarian crown)
properties.info: Croatia had been united with Hungary under Coloman from 1102 and kept its own ban and institutions. Venice and Hungary contested the Dalmatian cities, and Zadar fell to Venice in 1202. The existing Croatian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Bulgarian Empire
properties.info: The Asen brothers' revolt in 1185 restored Bulgaria, and Kaloyan ruled it from 1197. The existing Bulgarian polygons are a broad proxy; the realm's frontiers in Macedonia and Thrace changed constantly.

properties.label: Byzantium
properties.info: Alexios III seized the throne from his brother Isaac II in 1195. The empire had lost Bulgaria, Serbia, Cyprus and southern Italy and was weakened by internal division; the Fourth Crusade, which captured Constantinople in 1204, was still ahead. Existing Greek, Balkan and Anatolian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Zeta
properties.info: Duklja (Zeta) had been absorbed by Stefan Nemanja's Serbia by the 1180s and was ruled by Nemanja's son Vukan. Existing Montenegrin provinces are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Serbia
properties.info: Stefan Nemanja threw off Byzantine control and united the Serbian lands; his son Stefan Nemanjić succeeded him in 1196, with a rivalry with his brother Vukan. Existing Serbian and Kosovo provinces are broad proxies.
Ban Kulin ruled Bosnia from about 1180 until 1204, as a largely autonomous banate nominally under Hungarian or Byzantine overlordship. The existing Bosnian polygons are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Cuman khans and local steppe groups
properties.info: Pechenegs had been displaced by Cumans, who dominated the steppe and intervened in Rus', Bulgarian and Byzantine politics. The existing steppe and Danubian provinces are broad proxies for a mobile frontier.

properties.leader: Cuman and local coastal authorities; weak Byzantine claim
properties.info: Byzantine authority on the Crimean coast was largely nominal by 1200 and the steppe was Cuman-dominated. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Ayyubids
properties.info: Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, took Jerusalem in 1187 and united Egypt, Syria and parts of the Jazira. After his death (1193), his brother al-Adil I took power in Egypt by 1200 while family members ruled Damascus, Aleppo and other cities. The existing Egyptian, Levantine and Syrian provinces are broad proxies for a loosely coordinated family confederation.

properties.label: Aleppo
properties.info: Saladin's son az-Zahir Ghazi ruled Aleppo from 1193 as a semi-independent Ayyubid prince. Existing Syrian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Almohads
properties.info: The Almohads overthrew the Almoravids in the 1140s and took al-Andalus. Muhammad al-Nasir ruled from 1199, and his later defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) opened Andalusia to the Christians. The existing Moroccan, Algerian and southern Iberian provinces are broad proxies; Almohad authority in Ifriqiya and the south was uneven.

properties.label: Almohad Ifriqiya
properties.leader: Almohad governors; Banu Ghaniya raiders remained active
properties.info: The Almohads took Mahdia and Tunis in 1159–1160, ending Zirid and Norman rule. Almoravid-descended Banu Ghaniya raiders still disrupted the region. The existing Tunisian provinces are a coarse proxy.

properties.leader: Almohad governors and local Arab tribal authorities
properties.info: The inland and eastern Algerian-Tunisian provinces were nominally Almohad, while Hilalian Arab tribes held much real local power. The existing provinces are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Tripolitania
properties.leader: Local and Ayyubid-linked authorities; Almohad claim
