properties.info: The Banu Khazrun had fallen after Norman occupation of Tripoli and its recovery by the Almohads in 1160. By 1200 Qaraqush, a former Ayyubid officer, and Banu Ghaniya raiders contested the region with the Almohads. These broad Libyan districts are only a proxy.

properties.leader: Local Arab and Berber authorities; Ayyubid influence
properties.info: Cyrenaica was lightly governed under local tribal authorities with Ayyubid influence from Egypt. The existing coastal districts are broad proxies.

properties.label: Rus' principalities
properties.leader: Fragmented among Rurikid princes; Vsevolod III (Vladimir-Suzdal) and Roman Mstislavich (Galicia-Volhynia) were prominent
properties.info: By 1200 Rus' was divided into rival principalities under the Rurikids. Kyiv had lost its central power; Vladimir-Suzdal, Galicia-Volhynia and Chernigov were important. The existing Rus' provinces are a single broad proxy rather than a political unit.

properties.leader: Local Rurikid (Vseslavich) princes; individual ruler uncertain
properties.info: Polotsk remained a distinct Rus' principality under its own dynasty, and its rulers faced Baltic and German pressure on the Dvina. The existing Belarusian province is a broad proxy.

properties.leader: Alan princes under Georgian influence; individual ruler uncertain
properties.info: Alan princes had close ties to Georgia and Queen Tamar's second husband, David Soslan, was an Alan prince. The existing North Caucasian province is a broad proxy.

properties.label: Georgia
properties.info: Tamar (1184–1213) ruled a Georgian kingdom unified under the Bagratids, including Tbilisi, Kakheti and Abkhazia, and was at the height of Georgian power. Her Zakarid commanders took Armenian cities such as Ani around 1199–1201. The existing Georgian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Shirvanshahs under Georgian pressure; Arran under the Eldiguzid atabegs
properties.info: The Shirvanshahs ruled in Shirvan, and the Eldiguzid atabegs dominated Arran and Azerbaijan as nominal successors to the Seljuks. The existing Azerbaijani province is a broad proxy.

properties.leader: Zakarid princes (Georgian vassals) in the north; local Muslim and Armenian lords elsewhere
properties.info: Zakarid Armenian princes ruled northern Armenian lands as vassals of Queen Tamar, while Muslim dynasties such as the Saltuqids and Shah-Armens held parts of the west and south. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Angevin Empire
properties.leader: John (King of England, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, Count of Anjou)
properties.info: John became king in 1199 after Richard I's death and held England together with Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine, Poitou and Aquitaine, a conglomerate of lands that historians call the Angevin Empire. The French lands were held as fiefs of the French king, and Philip II conquered Normandy in 1204 and most of the rest by 1224. John also claimed overlordship over Wales, Ireland and Scotland. The existing provinces and Channel Islands are broad proxies.

properties.label: León
properties.info: León and Castile were separated again after Alfonso VII's death in 1157. Alfonso IX ruled León from 1188 and, with Castile, was at war and at peace in turn. The existing Spanish provinces are broad map proxies.

properties.label: Castile
properties.info: Alfonso VIII ruled Castile from 1158. His forces were defeated at Alarcos in 1195, but he conquered Álava and Gipuzkoa from Navarre in 1199–1200. The existing Spanish provinces are broad map proxies.

properties.label: Navarre
properties.info: Sancho VII became king of Navarre in 1194. Castile conquered Álava and Gipuzkoa in 1199–1200, leaving Navarre confined to the existing Navarre province proxy.

properties.label: Aragon
properties.info: The Kingdom of Aragon and County of Barcelona were united in 1137, and Aragon also held Roussillon. Pedro II ruled from 1196. The existing Spanish provinces are broad map proxies.

properties.label: Mallorca
properties.info: The Banu Ghaniya, an Almoravid remnant, ruled the Balearics until the Almohad conquest in 1203. The existing island polygon is a broad map reference.
Roussillon had passed to the Crown of Aragon in 1172. The existing Pyrénées-Orientales province is a rough map proxy.

properties.label: Portugal
properties.info: Afonso I was recognized as king in 1143 and 1179, and took Lisbon in 1147. Sancho I ruled from 1185, and Portugal held land up to the lower Tagus and Alentejo while the Almohads held the south. The existing Portuguese provinces are broad map proxies.
William I ruled Scotland from 1165 until 1214. The modern Scottish mainland is a broad proxy; royal authority was uneven in Galloway, the north and the west.
Ragnald ruled Mann and the Isles from 1187 under Norwegian overlordship, with growing pressure from Scotland and England.
Harald Maddadsson was earl of Orkney and held Caithness under Scotland. The existing Orkney and Shetland provinces are broad proxies.

Llywelyn ab Iorwerth was seizing control of Gwynedd in 1199–1200, with Gwenwynwyn ruling southern Powys. The existing provinces are only a broad proxy; Welsh and Marcher lordships varied with local war.
Gwenwynwyn ruled southern Powys (Powys Wenwynwyn) and was an important rival of Gwynedd.

properties.leader: Sons of the Lord Rhys (Gruffydd and Maelgwn ap Rhys)
properties.info: The Lord Rhys, who had dominated Deheubarth, died in 1197 and his sons disputed the succession. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Glamorgan passed through the Gloucester heiress to John. His marriage to Isabel of Gloucester was annulled around 1199–1200, but he kept control of the lordship.

properties.leader: Marcher lords (including William de Braose and William Marshal)
properties.info: The marcher lords held Gwent and Gwynllwg as semi-independent lordships under the English crown. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: John de Courcy in the east; Ua Néill and other Irish dynasties elsewhere
properties.info: John de Courcy conquered Down and Antrim in 1177, while much of Ulster remained in Irish hands. The existing province is a broad proxy.
Cathal Crobderg held Connacht after the 1198 death of Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, the last high king. The existing counties are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Leinster (Norman lordship)
properties.info: After the Norman invasion of 1169–71, Leinster passed to Strongbow and then, through marriage, to William Marshal in 1189. Norman lords controlled much of the region, while some Irish dynasties remained. The existing counties are a broad proxy.

properties.leader: Donnchad Cairprech Ua Briain (Thomond); MacCarthy kings (Desmond)
properties.info: Munster was divided between Ua Briain Thomond and the MacCarthys of Desmond, with growing Norman intrusion. The existing counties are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Meath (Norman lordship)
properties.info: Meath was granted to Hugh de Lacy in 1172, and Walter de Lacy held it from 1194. The existing counties are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Dublin (Lordship of Ireland)
properties.info: Henry II took Dublin in 1171-72, and it became the centre of the Lordship of Ireland. John held the title Lord of Ireland, and the English justiciar governed on his behalf. The existing counties are a broad proxy.

properties.leader: Judges of Cagliari, Arborea, Torres and Gallura; Pisan and Genoese influence
properties.info: Sardinia was divided into four judicates with growing Pisan and Genoese influence. The existing Sardinian provinces are a single broad proxy.
The Hasanid sharifs held Mecca, nominally within the Ayyubid sphere of influence. Qatada ibn Idris became sharif around 1200 (the dates are approximate). The existing province is a broad proxy.
Medina was held by the Husayni sharifs under shifting Ayyubid and Hasanid influence. The existing province is a broad proxy.

properties.label: Khwarazmians
properties.info: The Khwarazm-Shahs ended the Seljuk sultanate of Iraq in 1194. Tekish died in 1200 and was followed by Muhammad II. Eldiguzid atabegs still held Azerbaijan and Ismaili strongholds persisted. The existing Iranian provinces are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Abbasid Caliphate
properties.info: Caliph al-Nasir (1180–1225) restored real Abbasid power in central and southern Iraq after the decline of the Seljuks. The existing Iraqi provinces are broad proxies.

Kilij Arslan II (d. 1192) made Rum the main Turkish state in Anatolia, absorbing the Danishmendids by 1178 and defeating the Byzantines at Myriokephalon (1176). His sons contested the succession, and Rukn al-Din Suleiman II ruled in 1200. The remaining Turkish province polygons are used as broad proxies; western coastal areas were Byzantine and the Pontic coast and Cilicia are shown separately.

properties.label: Pontic coast
properties.leader: Local Pontic lords (Gabras family); weak Byzantine claim
properties.info: The Danishmendids were absorbed by Rum by 1178. The Pontic coast was held by local lords such as the Gabras family under a weak Byzantine claim before the Empire of Trebizond in 1204. The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

Bohemond III ruled Antioch until 1201, though the principality had lost most inland and coastal territories to Saladin in 1188 and the Armenians. Hatay is a rough proxy for the surviving principality.

properties.leader: Aimery of Lusignan (King of Cyprus and Jerusalem)
properties.label: Jerusalem (Acre)
properties.info: Saladin took Jerusalem in 1187. After the Third Crusade (1189–92) a Crusader kingdom survived along the coast with Acre as its capital. Aimery of Lusignan was king from 1197. The existing provinces are only a rough proxy for a narrow coastal strip.

properties.label: Brittany
properties.info: Brittany was ruled by Duchess Constance and her son Arthur I, who was supported by Philip II against John's claim. The existing French departments are broad proxies.

properties.label: Cyprus
properties.info: Cyprus broke away from Byzantium under Isaac Komnenos in 1185 and was conquered by Richard I in 1191. It became a Lusignan kingdom, and Aimery took the royal title in 1197.

properties.label: Corsica
properties.info: Corsica was divided between the rival Pisan and Genoese communes, with local lords holding substantial power. The existing departments are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Leo II (Leon I), crowned king of Armenia in 1198
properties.label: Cilicia
properties.info: The Armenian principality of Cilicia became a kingdom under Leo, crowned in 1198 with imperial and papal support. The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Tripoli
properties.info: The County of Tripoli survived the 1187 Ayyubid conquests under Bohemond IV, who was also linked to Antioch. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Artuqid emirs (Mardin, Hisn Kayfa) and Kurdish lords under Ayyubid influence; rulers uncertain
properties.label: Jazira lords
properties.info: Upper Mesopotamia and the south-eastern highlands were held by Artuqid emirs and Kurdish lords, with al-Adil's Ayyubids dominating the area. The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Saltuqid emir at Erzurum and Mengujekid emir at Erzincan; rulers uncertain
properties.label: Eastern emirates
properties.info: The Saltuqids of Erzurum and the Mengujekids of Erzincan were small Turkish emirates between Rum, Georgia and the Armenian lands. The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Mosul
properties.info: The Zengid atabegs held Mosul and northern Iraq, with Nur ad-Din Arslan Shah I ruling from 1193. Erbil and other cities were held by separate lords. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

1300.note: Around-1300 snapshot built on the 1200 map. Edward I had conquered Wales and England kept only Gascony in France; Philip IV ruled a consolidated France including Normandy, Anjou and Poitou. Castile and León were united, Aragon had Valencia, Portugal reached the Algarve, and only the Emirate of Granada remained Muslim in Iberia while the Marinids ruled Morocco, the Zayyanids Tlemcen and the Hafsids Tunisia. After the Sicilian Vespers (1282) Sicily was Aragonese and Naples was Angevin. Bohemia was a kingdom, the Teutonic and Livonian Orders held Prussia and Livonia, Lithuania was rising, and Galicia–Volhynia stood between Poland and the Golden Horde. Byzantium had been restored in 1261 but was reduced to Thrace and Macedonia, with Serbia expanding and Greece divided among Frankish, Venetian and Greek states. The Ilkhanate ruled Iran, Iraq and eastern Anatolia, the Mamluks had conquered the Crusader states by 1291, and the Ottoman beylik was just emerging. All borders are broad modern-region approximations, not medieval frontiers.

properties.info: Birger became king in 1290 under the regency of Torgils Knutsson, who built Vyborg castle in 1293 and extended Swedish rule in Finland, which had come under the crown through the crusades of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. The existing provinces are broad proxies; royal control in the north was weak.
Eric VI ruled from 1286, in conflict with the Church and the nobility, and had lost the Danish overlordship over the southern Baltic coast. The existing Danish provinces are broad proxies.
Haakon V ruled from 1299 and Norway was at its height, with Iceland and the Faroes under the crown since 1262–1264. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Iceland
properties.info: Iceland accepted the Norwegian king in 1262–1264 with the Old Covenant, ending the Commonwealth.
The Faroes were part of the Norwegian realm.

properties.leader: Haakon V (King of Norway); earls of Orkney
properties.info: Orkney and Shetland stayed Norwegian, while the Hebrides had been ceded to Scotland by the Treaty of Perth in 1266.

Albert I was king from 1298 after defeating Adolf of Nassau, and the Habsburgs were rising in Austria. The Empire was a loose union of princes and cities. Provence belonged to the Angevins of Naples, while Savoy, Dauphiné and the Rhône valley were still nominally imperial. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Mecklenburg
properties.info: Mecklenburg was a German lordship within the Empire after the Obotrite lands were Germanized. The existing polygon is a broad proxy that also covers Pomerania.

properties.leader: Otto IV and the Ascanian margraves
properties.info: Brandenburg was ruled jointly by the Ascanian margraves and expanded east of the Oder. The existing polygons are broad proxies.

properties.label: Bohemia
properties.info: Wenceslaus II ruled Bohemia and Moravia as king from 1278 and was crowned King of Poland in 1300. The Přemyslid dynasty died out in 1306. Existing Czech provinces are broad proxies.

Philip IV ruled a consolidated France that included Normandy, Anjou, Maine, Touraine and Poitou, annexed after 1204, and Champagne through his marriage. Gascony remained English and Brittany a separate duchy. Provence, Savoy and the Rhône valley are shown outside France as imperial lands, which is a simplification.
Brittany was a duchy under John II, a peer of France whose dukes were often allied with England. The existing Breton departments are broad proxies.

properties.label: England
properties.info: Edward I ruled England, conquered Wales in 1282–1284 and held Gascony as a fief of the French king. Normandy, Anjou and Poitou had been lost to France, and the Channel Islands stayed with the English crown. The Gascon departments and the Welsh counties are broad proxies.

properties.realm: Gaelic Ulster and the Earldom of Ulster
properties.label: Ulster
properties.leader: Richard de Burgh, Earl of Ulster; Ua Néill and other Gaelic lords
properties.info: The Earldom of Ulster covered the east coast under Richard de Burgh, while Gaelic dynasties held the interior. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Ua Conchobair kings under pressure from the de Burghs
properties.info: Connacht remained largely Gaelic under the Ua Conchobair dynasty, while the de Burghs pressed in from the east. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Scotland
properties.info: After the Wars of Independence began in 1296, Scotland was ruled by guardians while Edward I of England claimed overlordship. Robert Bruce was crowned in 1306. The existing Scottish provinces are broad proxies.
The Isle of Man passed from Norway to Scotland in 1266 and was contested between Scotland and England in the Wars of Independence.

properties.label: Poland (Piast duchies)
properties.leader: Wenceslaus II of Bohemia (crowned 1300) and Władysław the Elbow-high
properties.info: Poland was still divided among Piast duchies. Wenceslaus II of Bohemia was crowned King of Poland in 1300 and held Greater Poland and Kraków, with Władysław the Elbow-high contesting the crown. The existing Polish provinces remain one proxy.
The Yotvingians were crushed in the 1280s, and Sudovia was divided between Lithuanian and Polish influence and the Teutonic Order. The existing Podlaskie polygon is a broad proxy.

properties.label: Teutonic Order
properties.info: The Teutonic Order had conquered Prussia by 1283 and moved its headquarters to Marienburg in 1309. The existing Kaliningrad and Warmia–Masuria polygons are broad proxies.

properties.label: Livonian Order
properties.leader: Gottfried von Rogga, Master of Livonia
properties.info: The Livonian Order and the bishops ruled Livonia and Courland after the conquest of the Semigallians in 1290. The existing Latvian polygons are broad proxies.

properties.label: Danish Estonia
properties.info: Northern Estonia (Harria, Wierland and Jerwen) was Danish from 1219, with Reval as its centre. The existing Estonian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Lithuania
properties.info: Lithuania was unified under Mindaugas in the 1230s and by Vytenis (1295–1315) had expanded into western Rus'. It was a pagan state that resisted the Teutonic Order. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Rus' principalities
properties.leader: Rurikid princes under the Golden Horde (Vladimir, Tver, Moscow, Ryazan)
properties.info: After the Mongol conquest of 1237–1240, the Rus' principalities were Golden Horde tributaries. Vladimir was the senior throne, with Tver and Moscow rising rivals. Kyiv and southern Rus' were left in Mongol hands. The existing Russian and Belarusian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Golden Horde
properties.info: The Golden Horde (Ulus of Jochi) ruled the steppe from Sarai under Toqta (1291–1312) and held the Rus' princes as tributaries. Its control over the Black Sea steppe, southern Rus' and the lower Danube is shown as a broad proxy.
Volga Bulgaria had been conquered by the Mongols in 1236 and was part of the Golden Horde.
The Volga–Ural lands were part of the Golden Horde, as a broad proxy.
Alania was destroyed by the Mongols in the 1230s and the North Caucasus came under the Golden Horde.
The northern Caucasus plains were under the Golden Horde, with local mountain communities mostly outside its control.

properties.leader: Toqta Khan; Genoese colony at Caffa
properties.info: Crimea was under the Golden Horde, with Genoese trading colonies such as Caffa on the coast.
Polotsk was drawn into the Lithuanian sphere in the late thirteenth century.

Andrew III ruled from 1290 until his death in 1301, with the Árpád dynasty ending and local magnates holding much of the real power. Zakarpattia was part of the kingdom. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Andrew III; the Šubić family as bans
properties.info: Croatia stayed linked to the Hungarian crown, with the Šubić of Bribir ruling Dalmatia and Bosnia as powerful bans.
Bosnia was a banate under the overlordship of the Šubić family and Hungary, with the Kotromanić dynasty rising.
Theodore Svetoslav was tsar from 1300 after a period of Mongol and Nogai influence, and restored some stability. The existing Bulgarian polygons are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Serbia
properties.info: Milutin (1282–1321) pushed Serbia south to Skopje and northern Macedonia and expanded at Byzantium's expense, and Zeta was fully integrated. The Macedonian and Albanian municipalities are broad proxies.
Zeta was part of the Serbian kingdom under Milutin, with local nobles holding the coast.

properties.label: Byzantium
properties.info: Michael VIII recovered Constantinople in 1261 and Andronikos II (1282–1328) ruled a shrunken empire of Thrace, Macedonia and scattered holdings such as Berat, under pressure from Serbia, the Turkish beyliks and the Catalan threat. Epirus, Thessaly, Athens, Achaea and the Venetian islands were held by others. The existing Greek and Turkish provinces are broad proxies.
Boniface VIII (1294–1303) claimed supremacy over secular rulers and clashed with Philip IV of France. The existing central Italian provinces are broad proxies for papal lands.
Benevento remained a papal enclave on the border of the Kingdom of Naples; its existing provinces are a broad proxy.

properties.label: Sicily
properties.info: After the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 the island came under the House of Aragon. Frederick III ruled it from 1296 and held it against the Angevins of Naples in the War of the Vespers, confirmed by the Peace of Caltabellotta in 1302. The existing Sicilian provinces and Malta are broad proxies.

properties.label: Corsica
properties.info: Genoa had defeated Pisa at Meloria in 1284 and held most of Corsica. The existing Corsican departments are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Pisa, Genoa and the Judge of Arborea; Aragon enfeoffed in 1297
properties.info: Sardinia was divided among Pisa, Genoa and the Giudicato of Arborea, and the pope enfeoffed the Aragonese king with the island in 1297. The existing Sardinian provinces are a single proxy.

properties.leader: Joan I (Philip IV of France as consort)
properties.info: Navarre was united with the French crown through Joan I's marriage to Philip IV, though it kept its own institutions. The existing Navarrese province is a broad proxy.

properties.label: Castile and León
properties.leader: Ferdinand IV (regency of Maria de Molina)
properties.info: Castile and León were permanently united in 1230 under Ferdinand III, who also took Córdoba, Seville and Jaén. Ferdinand IV came to the throne in 1295 under his mother's regency. The existing Spanish provinces are broad proxies.

James I conquered Valencia and Majorca in 1229–1245. James II (1291–1327) held Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia, and Sicily passed to his brother Frederick. The existing Spanish provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Majorca
properties.info: The Kingdom of Majorca was created in 1262 for a younger line of the Aragonese house. It included the Balearics, Roussillon and Montpellier and was a vassal of Aragon. The existing polygons are broad proxies.
Portugal finished the conquest of the Algarve in 1249, and the Treaty of Alcanizes with Castile in 1297 fixed its borders. Denis ruled from 1279. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Marinids
properties.info: The Marinids replaced the Almohads in Morocco, taking Marrakesh in 1269. Abu Yaqub Yusuf ruled from 1286 and intervened in Iberia while besieging Tlemcen. The existing Moroccan provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Hafsids
properties.info: The Hafsids ruled Ifriqiya from Tunis and held a caliphal claim after 1259, with authority extending over eastern Algeria and Tripolitania. Their rule was weakened by succession struggles. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
The Tunisian interior and eastern Algeria were under Hafsid authority, with local Arab tribes holding much of the hinterland.

properties.leader: Hafsid governors and local tribal authorities
properties.info: Tripolitania was nominally Hafsid but held loosely by local authorities.
Cyrenaica was under local Arab tribes with Mamluk influence from Egypt.

properties.label: Mamluks
properties.info: The Mamluks ruled Egypt and Syria from Cairo after taking power in 1250 and defeating the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260. al-Nasir Muhammad ruled from 1293. They conquered the last Crusader strongholds, Acre in 1291. Existing provinces are broad proxies.
Aleppo was a Mamluk province and the northern frontier against the Ilkhanate and Cilician Armenia.
Antioch fell to the Mamluks in 1268 and the principality ended.
Acre fell to the Mamluks in 1291, ending the Crusader kingdom on the mainland; its titular kings were then in Cyprus.
Tripoli fell to the Mamluks in 1289.
Henry II ruled Cyprus and held the nominal title of King of Jerusalem, and Cyprus became the main Latin base in the east after 1291. The existing Cypriot provinces are broad proxies.
Cilician Armenia was a Mongol ally and a frequent target of Mamluk raids, ruled by Hetoum II (1289–1305). The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Rum (Ilkhanid)
properties.info: Rum was an Ilkhanid protectorate after the Mongol victory at Köse Dağ in 1243. Real power lay with Mongol governors and the Turkoman beyliks on the frontier. The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Trebizond
properties.info: The Komnenian empire of Trebizond survived on the Black Sea coast, a vassal of the Ilkhanate. The existing Pontic provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Ilkhanate
properties.info: The Mongol Ilkhanate ruled Persia, Iraq and the Caucasus from Tabriz. Ghazan (1295–1304) converted to Islam and reformed the administration, and fought the Mamluks over Syria. The existing Iranian provinces are a broad proxy.
Baghdad was destroyed by the Mongols in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate there. Iraq was an Ilkhanid province.
Mosul and northern Iraq were Ilkhanid provinces after the Mongol conquests.

properties.leader: Ghazan; local Artuqid emirs as vassals
properties.info: Upper Mesopotamia was under Ilkhanid control, with Artuqid emirs in Mardin as vassals.
The Erzurum region was under Ilkhanid rule.

properties.leader: Ghazan; Armenian and Georgian local lords as vassals
properties.info: Armenia was under the Ilkhanate, with local Armenian lords as vassals.
Arran was an Ilkhanid province and Shirvan a vassal dynasty.
Georgia was an Ilkhanid vassal after 1246 and was split in two for a time, with David VIII reuniting it from 1293 to 1311. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Granada
properties.info: The Nasrid emirate of Granada was founded by Muhammad I in 1238 and survived as a vassal of Castile. It held Granada, Málaga and Almería, a broad proxy.

properties.label: Zayyanids
properties.info: The Zayyanids ruled Tlemcen and the central Maghreb, caught between the Marinids, who besieged Tlemcen from 1299, and the Hafsids. The existing Algerian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Provence
properties.leader: Charles II of Anjou (Count of Provence)
properties.info: Provence passed to Charles of Anjou in 1246 through his marriage and was held by the Angevin kings of Naples as a fief of the Empire. Vaucluse (the Comtat Venaissin) was in fact a papal possession. The existing French departments are broad proxies.

properties.label: Naples
properties.info: Charles of Anjou took the Kingdom of Sicily in 1266, but lost the island in the Sicilian Vespers of 1282. His son Charles II (1285–1309) ruled the mainland from Naples, with a claim to Albania and Corfu. The mainland provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Galicia–Volhynia
properties.info: Galicia–Volhynia was the strongest western Rus' principality, tributary to the Golden Horde and disputed by Poland, Hungary and Lithuania. Yuri I ruled from 1301. The existing Ukrainian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Novgorod
properties.leader: Posadnik and veche; Alexander Nevsky's descendants as princes
properties.info: Novgorod was a merchant republic governed by the veche and a posadnik, with a prince invited from Vladimir, and held a large northern trade empire. The existing Russian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Gottfried von Rogga, Master of Livonia; bishops of Dorpat and Ösel–Wiek
properties.info: Southern Estonia and the islands were held by the Livonian Order and the bishoprics of Dorpat and Ösel–Wiek. The existing Estonian provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Epirus
properties.info: The Despotate of Epirus was a Greek state in the west, a rival of Byzantium, ruled under Angevin and Byzantine pressure by Thomas I (1296–1318). The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Thessaly
properties.info: Thessaly was an independent Greek principality under John II Doukas, with a Vlach and Greek population. The existing Thessalian province is a broad proxy.

properties.label: Athens
properties.info: The Frankish Duchy of Athens was ruled by the de la Roche family, with Thebes as its centre, until the Catalan Company seized it in 1311. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Achaea
properties.leader: Isabella of Villehardouin and Florent of Hainault under Angevin overlordship
properties.info: The Frankish Principality of Achaea held most of the Peloponnese under the House of Anjou, while Byzantium held the south-east around Mystras. The existing Peloponnese province is a broad proxy.

properties.label: Venetian Crete
properties.leader: Republic of Venice; Genoese, Byzantine and Frankish lords in the islands
properties.info: Venice held Crete, while the Cyclades formed the Frankish Duchy of the Archipelago under Venetian patronage and the Dodecanese were still Byzantine or Genoese until the Hospitallers took Rhodes in 1309. The existing island provinces cannot separate these and show them together.

properties.label: Turkish beyliks
properties.leader: Osman I, Karasi, Aydin, Menteshe and Germiyan beys
properties.info: Turkoman beyliks arose on the Byzantine frontier as the Seljuk and Ilkhanid hold weakened. Osman's beylik near Söğüt and Bursa was just emerging, with Karasi, Saruhan, Aydin, Menteshe, Germiyan and Hamid to the south. The existing Turkish provinces are broad proxies.

1400.note: Around-1400 snapshot built on the 1300 map. The Kalmar Union (1397) joined Denmark, Norway and Sweden under Margaret and Eric of Pomerania. Poland had taken Galicia and was joined to Lithuania through Jogaila (1385), and Lithuania under Vytautas reached the Black Sea steppe; the Teutonic Order held Prussia, Estonia (bought 1346) and Gotland (1398). France under Charles VI was in the Hundred Years' War truce while Burgundy rose as a great power, England was ruled by Henry IV, Aragon held Sicily and Sardinia, and Portugal under John I had secured independence at Aljubarrota (1385). Northern Italy was dominated by Milan, Venice, Florence and Genoa. The Ottomans under Bayezid I had conquered Bulgaria, Thessaly and most of Anatolia and besieged Constantinople, leaving Byzantium a rump; Timur was about to overrun Iran, Iraq and Syria, and the Mamluks ruled Egypt and Syria. All borders are broad modern-region approximations, not medieval frontiers.

properties.label: Kalmar Union
properties.leader: Margaret I (regent) and Eric of Pomerania
properties.info: The Kalmar Union of 1397 joined Denmark, Norway and Sweden (with Finland) under Margaret I of Denmark, who ruled for her grand-nephew Eric of Pomerania. The union was a personal one and the three kingdoms kept their own laws. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Margaret I and Eric of Pomerania
properties.info: Iceland passed with the Norwegian crown into the Kalmar Union in 1397 and was governed by royal officials and the Althing.

properties.leader: Margaret I and Eric of Pomerania
properties.info: The Faroes belonged to the Norwegian crown and so to the Kalmar Union.
The Teutonic Order took Gotland in 1398 to suppress the Victual Brothers' piracy and held it until 1408.

properties.leader: Wennemar von Brüggenei, Master of Livonia; bishops of Dorpat and Ösel–Wiek
properties.info: Denmark sold northern Estonia to the Teutonic Order in 1346, and it passed to the Livonian branch. All of Estonia was held by the Order and the bishoprics. The existing Estonian provinces are broad proxies.

The Order was at its height under Conrad von Jungingen (1393–1407), with Prussia, Pomerelia, Gotland and Estonia, but Lithuania's baptism in 1386 had removed its crusading rationale. The existing polygons are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Wennemar von Brüggenei, Master of Livonia
properties.info: The Livonian Order and the bishops ruled Livonia and Courland. The existing Latvian polygons are broad proxies.

properties.label: Poland
properties.leader: Władysław II Jagiełło (also Grand Duke of Lithuania) and Queen Jadwiga's heritage
properties.info: Poland was reunited under Casimir III, who took Galicia (Red Ruthenia) in 1340–1349. After the Union of Krewo (1385) Jogaila of Lithuania ruled as Władysław II, in union with Lithuania. Silesia was under Bohemian overlordship. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Vytautas the Great (Grand Duke) under Jogaila
properties.info: Lithuania had grown into a great Rus' empire from the Baltic toward the Black Sea, including Kyiv, Volhynia and Podolia. Vytautas ruled from 1392 and was about to be beaten by the Golden Horde at Vorskla in 1399. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Vasily I of Moscow, Dmitri's son; other Rurikid princes
properties.info: Moscow had grown through Dmitri Donskoy's victory at Kulikovo (1380) and led the Rus' principalities, though they still paid tribute to the Golden Horde after Tokhtamysh sacked Moscow in 1382. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Timur Qutlugh, with the emir Edigu
properties.info: The Golden Horde was shattered by Timur's campaigns of 1391 and 1395 against Tokhtamysh and dominated by the emir Edigu, and it soon broke up. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Brandenburg passed to the Luxembourg dynasty in 1373, and Jobst of Moravia ruled it from 1388. The Neumark was pledged to the Teutonic Order in 1402. The existing polygons are broad proxies.

Bohemia was the centre of the Luxembourg dynasty, and Wenceslaus IV was also King of the Romans until deposed in 1400. Charles IV had founded Prague University in 1348 and taken Silesia in 1335–1348; Jan Hus was beginning to preach. The existing Czech provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Rupert of the Palatinate (elected 1400; Wenceslaus deposed)
properties.info: The Empire was a loose federation. Wenceslaus IV was deposed by the electors in August 1400 and Rupert of the Palatinate elected in his place. Northern Italy had effectively left imperial control, and the Visconti held a ducal title from the emperor (1395). Borders are very broad proxies.

Charles VI (1380–1422) was subject to bouts of madness, and the rivalry between the Burgundian and Orléans factions was growing. A truce with England was in force, with Calais and Gascony still English. Savoy and Provence are shown separately, which is a simplification.

properties.label: Burgundy
properties.info: Philip the Bold, son of John II of France, received the Duchy of Burgundy in 1363 and gained Flanders, Artois and Franche-Comté through his marriage in 1384, building a state that rivalled the French crown. The existing polygons are broad proxies.
Brittany had won independence in the War of the Breton Succession (1364) and John V ruled from 1399 as a duke balancing between France and England.
Provence was held by the second Angevin house, Louis II of Anjou, who also claimed the Kingdom of Naples.

Henry IV of Lancaster took the throne in 1399 after deposing Richard II. England held Calais and Gascony and its Irish lordship, while Owain Glyndŵr's revolt in Wales was about to begin. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Robert III (1390–1406) ruled under the influence of his brother the Duke of Albany. Scotland was allied with France against England.

Henry III ruled from 1390 under the Trastámara dynasty, which took the throne in 1369. Castile was the largest Iberian kingdom and was preparing to raid Granada and the Canaries. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Charles III ruled from 1387 and made peace with Castile and Aragon after a long period of French and English influence.

John I won the throne in 1385 and defeated Castile at Aljubarrota. The Treaty of Windsor (1386) allied Portugal with England, and Ceuta was soon to be attacked (1415). The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Granada under the Nasrids was the last Muslim state in Iberia and was a tributary of Castile. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

Martin I ruled from 1396 and held Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, Majorca and Roussillon, while his son ruled Sicily. Sardinia was mostly Aragonese except for the Judicate of Arborea. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Sardinia was conquered by Aragon from 1323 and held in 1400 except for the Judicate of Arborea, which was still resisting.

properties.leader: Martin I of Sicily (son of Martin the Humane)
properties.info: Sicily had been held by a cadet Aragonese line since the Vespers, and after 1392 was ruled by Martin the Younger, with the island effectively tied to Aragon.

properties.label: Genoa
properties.leader: Doge Antoniotto Adorno; French protectorate from 1396
properties.info: Genoa was a maritime republic with colonies in the Black Sea and Aegean, and it put itself under French protection in 1396. It held Liguria and Corsica. The existing polygons are broad proxies.
The Western Schism (1378–1417) divided the papacy between Rome and Avignon. Boniface IX had reasserted control over the Papal States around Rome.
Naples was contested between the Durazzo line under Ladislaus and the Angevins of Provence under Louis II. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Venice held Crete, the Aegean islands and trading ports.

Sigismund ruled from 1387, and was soon to lose the Battle of Nicopolis (1396) to the Ottomans. Hungary held Croatia and Dalmatia and shared the Danube frontier with Wallachia and Serbia. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Croatia remained in union with Hungary, with Bosnia pressing on the south and Venice holding Dalmatian coastal towns.

properties.label: Bosnia
properties.info: Bosnia became a kingdom in 1377 under Tvrtko I and was at its widest under him, but after Kosovo (1389) it was threatened by the Ottomans.

properties.label: Serbia
properties.info: After Kosovo (1389) Serbia under Prince Lazar's son Stefan Lazarević became an Ottoman vassal, and fought for Bayezid at Nicopolis. The existing polygons are broad proxies.
Tarnovo fell to the Ottomans in 1393 and Vidin in 1396, ending the Bulgarian state.
Thrace, Macedonia and Thessalonica were taken by the Ottomans in the 1360s–1390s. Rumelia was the Ottomans' European province.

properties.label: Byzantine Empire
properties.leader: Manuel II Palaiologos (emperor); Theodore I (Despot of the Morea)
properties.info: Byzantium was reduced to Constantinople, which Bayezid I was blockading, and the Despotate of the Morea at Mistra. Manuel II (1391) sought help in the West. The existing polygons are broad proxies.
Thessaly came under Ottoman rule in 1394.
The Florentine Acciaioli family took Athens in 1388 from the Catalans' successors.

properties.leader: Esau de' Buondelmonti, with Albanian clans
properties.info: Epirus was split among Albanian and Italian lords, with the Ottomans pressing from the east.

properties.label: Ottoman Empire
properties.info: Bayezid I (1389–1402) expanded the Ottoman state over most of Anatolia and the Balkans, crushing the Crusaders at Nicopolis (1396) and blockading Constantinople. Timur's invasion in 1402 would break it. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Bayezid absorbed Karaman and central Anatolia in 1390–1398. The existing polygons are broad proxies.
Trebizond kept its independence on the Black Sea coast as a vassal of Timur's neighbours.
The Lusignan kingdom was weakened by Genoese occupation of Famagusta (1373) and was a tributary of the Mamluks.
The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia fell to the Mamluks in 1375.
The Burji Mamluks held Egypt and Syria. Faraj was a child sultan from 1399, and Timur's invasion of Syria in 1400–1401 was about to occur.
Aleppo was a Mamluk province on the northern frontier, and was sacked by Timur in 1400.
Part of the Mamluk Sultanate.
Part of the Mamluk Sultanate.
Part of the Mamluk Sultanate.

properties.label: Timurid Empire
properties.info: Timur had conquered Persia (1381–1387) and built an empire from Central Asia, and was about to invade Anatolia and Syria. The existing Iranian polygon is a broad proxy.
Armenia and the Caucasus were devastated by Timur's campaigns of 1386–1403.
Shirvan was a Timurid vassal under the Shirvanshahs.

properties.label: Jalayirid Sultanate
properties.info: The Jalayirids ruled Iraq and Azerbaijan from Baghdad and Tabriz and were driven out by Timur in 1393 and 1401. The existing polygons are broad proxies.
Northern Iraq and the Jazira were contested between the Jalayirids and the Turkmen.
Upper Mesopotamia was a mix of Jalayirid, Aq Qoyunlu and Mamluk influence.
Eastern Anatolia was held by Turkmen emirs after the Ilkhanate collapsed; the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu were rising.
Georgia was devastated by Timur's invasions (1386–1403) and lost its unity.
The Marinid state was in decline, with viziers ruling for child sultans, and Fez was losing control of the interior.
The Hafsids under Abu Faris (1394–1434) restored central authority in Ifriqiya after a period of fragmentation.
The Zayyanid kingdom of Tlemcen was weak and often a vassal of the Marinids or Hafsids.

properties.label: Milan
properties.info: Gian Galeazzo Visconti became Duke of Milan in 1395 and expanded over Lombardy, Veneto and Tuscany by 1400, threatening Florence. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Venice
properties.info: Venice was a maritime republic with its main land holdings in the Veneto beginning with Treviso (1339); the Aegean and Crete were shown separately. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Florence
properties.info: Florence led the Tuscan resistance to Milan and had won Arezzo in 1384. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Savoy
properties.info: The Counts of Savoy controlled the Alpine passes and Piedmont, and Amadeus VII gained Nice in 1388. Amadeus VIII was count from 1391. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Italian signorie
properties.leader: Gonzaga, Este, Carrara, Guinigi and others
properties.info: Small states ruled by local families such as the Gonzaga at Mantua, the Este at Ferrara and Modena, the Carrara at Padua, and Lucca under the Guinigi, caught between Milan and Venice.
The Teutonic Order had taken Pomerelia and Danzig in 1308–1309.

properties.label: Pomerania
properties.info: Pomerania was ruled by the Griffin dukes and was a fief of the Holy Roman Empire. The existing polygon is a broad proxy.

properties.leader: Wenceslaus IV of Luxembourg; Piast dukes as vassals
properties.info: The Silesian Piast duchies became fiefs of the Bohemian crown in 1335–1348.

properties.label: Moldavia
properties.info: Moldavia was founded in the 1350s–1360s as a principality between Hungary and the Golden Horde, and by 1400 was a tributary of Poland. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Wallachia
properties.info: Wallachia under Mircea the Elder (1386–1418) held Dobruja and fought the Ottomans at Rovine (1395), before becoming their tributary. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

1500.note: Around-1500 snapshot built on the 1400 map. Sweden had left the Kalmar Union in practice, leaving Denmark–Norway under John I, while Moscow under Ivan III had swallowed Novgorod (1478) and Tver (1485) and shaken off the Horde (1480). The Golden Horde had broken into the Crimean Khanate (an Ottoman vassal since 1475), the Great Horde, Kazan and the Nogai; the Teutonic Order had lost West Prussia to Poland (1466). Ferdinand and Isabella had conquered Granada (1492), France had absorbed Burgundy, Brittany and Provence, and Maximilian's Habsburg house held the Burgundian Netherlands. The Ottomans under Bayezid II had taken Constantinople, Serbia, Bosnia, the Morea, Albania and Trebizond, while Venice held Cyprus. Safavid Iran was just emerging (1501) beside the Aq Qoyunlu, and the Mamluks still ruled Egypt and Syria. All borders are broad modern-region approximations, not medieval frontiers.

properties.label: Denmark–Norway
properties.info: After the Stockholm Bloodbath and decades of rebellions, Sweden left the Kalmar Union in practice under the regents Sten Sture and Svante Nilsson. John I (Hans) ruled Denmark and Norway, and briefly Sweden in 1497–1501. Skåne, Halland and Blekinge were Danish.

properties.leader: John I of Denmark and Norway
properties.info: Iceland belonged to the Danish-Norwegian crown, governed by royal officials and the Althing, with English and German traders active along the coast.

properties.leader: John I of Denmark and Norway
John I of Denmark and Norway
properties.info: Gotland passed from the Teutonic Order to Denmark in 1449 under Christopher of Bavaria's successor, Christian I, after the Victual Brothers' pirate era.

After the Thirteen Years' War the Peace of Toruń (1466) gave West Prussia to Poland and made the Order's remaining Prussian state a Polish fief. Frederick of Saxony became Grand Master in 1498 and resisted this vassalage.
Royal Prussia, with Gdańsk, Toruń and Elbląg, joined Poland in 1466 after the Thirteen Years' War.
Poland under the Jagiellonians ruled through the nobility's Sejm, was in a loose union with Lithuania and had won Royal Prussia in 1466. The Nihil novi constitution followed in 1505.
Lithuania under Alexander Jagiellon was in personal union with Poland, and was losing its eastern border lands to Moscow in the wars that began in 1492 and 1500.

properties.label: Grand Duchy of Moscow
properties.info: Ivan III gathered the Russian lands, annexing Novgorod (1478) and Tver (1485), and ended the Tatar yoke at the Ugra (1480). He began to call himself sovereign of all Rus' and took the Byzantine double-headed eagle after marrying Sophia Palaiologina.
Novgorod lost its independence to Moscow after the Battle of Shelon (1471) and was annexed in 1478, and its veche bell was carried off to Moscow.

properties.label: Crimean Khanate
properties.info: The Crimean Khanate under the Giray dynasty broke away from the Golden Horde in the 1440s, and became an Ottoman vassal in 1475. Its raiders took slaves from Poland-Lithuania and Moscow, and in 1502 it destroyed the Great Horde. The steppe borders are broad proxies.

properties.label: Kazan
properties.info: The Khanate of Kazan arose in 1438 from the Golden Horde on the middle Volga. Moscow repeatedly intervened in its succession, and installed Muhammad Amin as khan in 1487.

properties.label: Nogai Horde
properties.info: The Nogai Horde, a nomadic confederation under Edigu's descendants, roamed the steppe between the Volga and the Ural and between the Siberian and Kazan khanates.

The Hundred Years' War ended in 1453, with England driven from all of France except Calais. Louis XI took Burgundy and Picardy (1477), Anjou, Maine and Provence (1481), and Charles VIII gained Brittany by marriage in 1491, before invading Italy in 1494.
Brittany's heiress Anne married Charles VIII in 1491, and then Louis XII in 1499, binding the duchy to France.
Provence was bequeathed to the French crown by Charles of Maine in 1481.

properties.label: Burgundian Netherlands
properties.info: After Charles the Bold died at Nancy (1477), Louis XI took the Duchy of Burgundy itself. His daughter Mary's marriage to Maximilian of Habsburg passed the Netherlands, Artois and Franche-Comté to the Habsburgs, and Philip the Handsome ruled them from 1494.
Granada fell to Ferdinand and Isabella on 2 January 1492, ending Muslim rule in Iberia. Columbus sailed the same year.

properties.leader: Isabella I (with Ferdinand II of Aragon)
properties.info: Isabella and Ferdinand's marriage in 1469 joined Castile and Aragon in a dynastic union, which kept separate laws and institutions. They conquered Granada (1492) and sponsored Columbus.
Ferdinand II ruled Aragon, Catalonia and Valencia, as well as Sicily and Sardinia, and regained Roussillon in 1493. His marriage to Isabella of Castile started the union of the Spanish crowns.

properties.leader: Catherine and John III of Albret

properties.info: Portugal under Manuel I was at the start of its golden age: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, and Cabral reached Brazil in 1500.
Henry VII founded the Tudor dynasty by winning at Bosworth (1485), which ended the Wars of the Roses. England held Calais and Ireland's Pale, and Henry rebuilt royal finances and order.
Orkney and Shetland passed to Scotland in 1468–69 as the dowry of Margaret of Denmark.
Man was held by the Stanley family under the English crown.

properties.label: Gaelic Ireland
properties.leader: Ua Néill and other Gaelic lords
properties.info: Outside the Pale, most of Ireland was ruled by Gaelic and Gaelicised Norman lords. Provinces are broad proxies.

properties.leader: Ua Conchobair and de Burgh (Burke) lords
properties.info: Outside the Pale, most of Ireland was ruled by Gaelic and Gaelicised Norman lords. Provinces are broad proxies.

Hungary under Matthias Corvinus (1458–1490) reached its late medieval peak, with Vienna taken in 1485. Under the weak Jagiellon Vladislaus II the nobles' power grew, while the Ottomans pressed on the southern frontier.
Venice took Cyprus in 1489, when Queen Catherine Cornaro was made to abdicate.

properties.leader: Walter von Plettenberg, Master of Livonia
Walter von Plettenberg, Master of Livonia

properties.info: Stephen the Great (1457–1504) defended Moldavia against the Ottomans at Vaslui (1475), but accepted Ottoman suzerainty in 1486.
The Ottomans conquered Bosnia in 1463 and Herzegovina in 1482.
Serbia was fully annexed by the Ottomans after the fall of Smederevo in 1459.
Albanian resistance under Skanderbeg ended after his death in 1468, and Shkodër fell in 1479.
Athens fell to Mehmed II in 1458, and the Morea followed in 1460.
Mehmed II conquered Constantinople on 29 May 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and made it the Ottoman capital. The Morea was taken in 1460.
Trebizond, the last Greek successor state, fell to Mehmed II in 1461.

After Mehmed the Conqueror took Constantinople (1453), the Ottomans absorbed Serbia, Bosnia, Albania, the Morea, Trebizond and Karaman, and made Crimea a vassal. Bayezid II (1481–1512) consolidated the empire and took the Venetian Morea ports in 1499–1500.

properties.leader: Mamluk sultans; Dulkadir and Ramadanid vassals
Mamluk sultans (Qaitbay d. 1496; Qansuh al-Ghawri from 1501)

properties.label: Safavid Iran
properties.info: Shah Ismail I took Tabriz from the Aq Qoyunlu in 1501 and founded the Safavid dynasty, making Twelver Shi'ism the state religion. The Timurids kept only Khorasan in the east. The borders are broad proxies.

properties.label: Aq Qoyunlu
properties.info: The Aq Qoyunlu (White Sheep Turkmen) under Uzun Hasan beat the Ottomans' rivals and the Black Sheep, and ruled Iraq, Armenia and western Iran. After Uzun Hasan's death in 1478 the state fell into civil wars, and the Safavids crushed it in 1501–1508.

properties.label: Wattasids
properties.info: The Wattasid viziers took over from the Marinids in 1472, and ruled Morocco while the Portuguese held Ceuta, Tangier and Atlantic coastal forts. The Saadians began their rise in the south.

properties.leader: Hafsid governors and local tribal authorities
Constantine II (Kartli) and rival Bagratid kings
properties.info: Georgia was split in the 1460s–1490 into the kingdoms of Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti and the princely Samtskhe, while the Ottomans and Aq Qoyunlu pressed in. The shown polygon is a single broad proxy.

properties.label: Sweden
properties.info: Sweden, with Finland, was ruled by regents from the Sture family after its victory at Brunkeberg (1471) and effectively stood outside the Kalmar Union. John I of Denmark briefly held the throne in 1497–1501. The existing provinces are broad proxies.
Moscow's frontier toward the steppe advanced south as the Upper Oka princes and the Seversk lands came under Ivan III. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

properties.label: Great Horde
properties.info: The Great Horde, the Golden Horde's direct heir on the lower Volga, failed to subdue Moscow at the Ugra (1480). The Crimean Khanate destroyed it in 1502. The Astrakhan Khanate split off in the 1460s. The existing provinces are broad proxies.

1600.note: Europe around 1600: the Ottoman Empire has swallowed the Mamluks, North Africa and central Hungary; Russia has taken the Volga khanates; Poland and Lithuania are united; Spain rules Italy and the Low Countries' south; the Reformation has split the Empire.

properties.info: The small duchies of northern Italy, such as Mantua, Modena, Parma and Lucca, lived in the shadow of Spanish Lombardy.
Michael the Brave rebelled against the Ottomans in 1594 and briefly united Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia in 1599-1600.

properties.leader: Michael the Brave (1600); then Ieremia Movila
properties.info: Moldavia was an Ottoman tributary principality, briefly united with Wallachia and Transylvania by Michael the Brave in 1600.

properties.leader: Bogislaw XIII and other Griffin dukes
properties.info: Pomerania was ruled by the Griffin dynasty until it died out in 1637.
The Duchy of Savoy, with Piedmont, balanced between France and Spain and gained Saluzzo from France in 1601.
Genoa was an oligarchic merchant republic allied to Spain; Genoese bankers financed the Habsburgs.
Benevento was a papal enclave inside the Spanish-ruled Kingdom of Naples.

properties.leader: Dukes of Mecklenburg (Schwerin and Gustrow lines)
properties.info: Mecklenburg was a Lutheran duchy of the Empire, divided among Schwerin and Gustrow lines.
Brandenburg under the Hohenzollerns was a Protestant electorate of the Empire, in personal union with the Duchy of Prussia from 1618.
Under Mehmed III (1595-1603) the Ottomans were fighting the Habsburgs in the Long Turkish War (1593-1606) and held the Balkans, central Hungary, Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt and North Africa.

properties.label: Tsardom of Russia
properties.info: Ivan IV took Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556) and began the conquest of Siberia. Boris Godunov became tsar in 1598 as the Rurik line ended, and the Time of Troubles followed.
Kazan fell to Ivan IV in 1552 and was annexed.
Astrakhan was annexed by Russia in 1556, giving it the whole Volga.
The Crimean Khanate was an Ottoman vassal and raided deep into Russia and Poland.
The Nogai Horde roamed the steppe between the Volga and the Ural and was being pushed into Russian and Ottoman-Crimean orbits.

properties.label: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
properties.info: The Union of Lublin (1569) merged Poland and Lithuania into one Commonwealth with an elected king.

properties.label: Prussia
properties.info: Grand Master Albert converted the Order's Prussia into a secular Lutheran duchy under Polish overlordship in 1525.
After the Livonian Order dissolved (1561), Livonia passed to Poland–Lithuania.
Northern Estonia submitted to Sweden in 1561.
Sweden under the Vasas became Lutheran and expanded into Estonia, but was in conflict with Poland over the crown.
Denmark–Norway under Christian IV was the leading Baltic power alongside Sweden.
Selim I conquered Syria and Egypt in 1516–17 and ended the Mamluk Sultanate.
The Ottomans took Tunis for good in 1574.
Algiers became an Ottoman regency from 1517 and Tlemcen was absorbed.
Baghdad fell to Suleiman in 1534.
Under Abbas I (1588–1629) Safavid Iran was reorganised and recovered land from the Ottomans and Uzbeks.
The Ottomans conquered Cyprus in 1570–71.

properties.label: Saadians
properties.info: The Saadi dynasty replaced the Wattasids and defeated Portugal at Alcácer Quibir (1578).

properties.label: Spain
properties.info: Castile, Aragon and, from 1580 to 1640, Portugal's empire were united under the Habsburg kings of Spain.
Upper Navarre was annexed by Castile in 1512–1515.
Portugal was in personal union with Spain from 1580.

properties.label: Tuscany
properties.info: The Medici became Grand Dukes of Tuscany in 1569.

properties.label: Spanish Netherlands
properties.info: The northern provinces revolted and formed the Dutch Republic; the south stayed under Spanish Habsburg rule.
The Empire was split between Catholics and Protestants after the Reformation and the Peace of Augsburg (1555).
Henry IV ended the Wars of Religion with the Edict of Nantes (1598).
England under Elizabeth I defeated the Spanish Armada (1588) and was conquering Ireland.
Connacht was brought under English control in the Elizabethan conquest.
Ulster resisted in the Nine Years' War (1594–1603).

properties.label: Bohemia
properties.info: Bohemia was ruled by the Habsburgs from 1526.

properties.leader: Alexander II of Kakheti, among rival Georgian kings

properties.label: Royal Hungary
properties.info: After Mohács (1526) Hungary was split in three: Habsburg Royal Hungary in the west and north, Ottoman Hungary in the centre and south, and Transylvania in the east.
Gascony was French after the Hundred Years War, and Dauphiné and Lyonnais were long part of the French crown.
The southern provinces stayed under Spanish Habsburg rule.

properties.label: Dutch Republic
properties.info: The seven northern provinces broke from Spain in the Dutch Revolt and declared independence in 1581.
Buda fell in 1541 and the Ottomans held central Hungary and the Banat as the Eyalet of Buda and Temesvár.

properties.label: Transylvania
properties.info: Transylvania became an autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty after 1541.

1700.note: Europe around 1700: Habsburg Austria has reconquered Hungary from the Ottomans (Karlowitz, 1699); France under Louis XIV has taken Alsace, Franche-Comté and Artois; Sweden is at its peak around the Baltic; Brandenburg–Prussia is rising; the Dutch Republic is a great power; Spain's Habsburg line is about to end.

properties.leader: Rival Georgian kings under Safavid and Ottoman suzerainty
properties.info: Georgia was split into Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti, fought over by Iran and the Ottomans.

properties.leader: Nogai beys (Russian, Kalmyk and Crimean pressure)
properties.info: The Nogais roamed the steppe between the Don and the Ural, squeezed by Russia, the Kalmyks and Crimea.
The Crimean Khanate was an Ottoman vassal that raided Ukraine and Russia for slaves.
The small duchies of northern Italy, such as Mantua, Modena, Parma and Lucca, were pawns in the struggle between Habsburgs and Bourbons.
Wallachia flourished culturally under Constantin Brancoveanu (1688-1714) while paying tribute to the Ottomans.
Moldavia was an Ottoman tributary principality ruled by hospodars appointed from Constantinople.
Farther Pomerania went to Brandenburg after the Griffin dynasty died out in 1637 and the Peace of Westphalia (1648); the west went to Sweden.
Savoy-Piedmont under Victor Amadeus II was an expanding Alpine state, soon to become a kingdom (Sicily 1713, Sardinia 1720).
Genoa was an oligarchic merchant republic with Corsica, in decline against Savoy and France.
Benevento was a papal enclave inside the Spanish-ruled Kingdom of Naples.
The Ottomans lost Hungary, Transylvania and Podolia at Karlowitz (1699); Mustafa II ruled 1695-1703.
Peter the Great was modernising Russia and about to challenge Sweden in the Great Northern War (from 1700). Left-bank Ukraine and Kyiv were Russian after 1667.
The Commonwealth recovered from the Deluge and the Ottoman wars but was weakening under its elective monarchy.
Sweden took Livonia from Poland in 1621–29 and held it by the Treaty of Oliva (1660).
Brandenburg-Prussia became sovereign in Prussia in 1657 and Frederick III crowned himself King in Prussia in 1701.

properties.label: Brandenburg–Prussia
properties.info: Brandenburg-Prussia under the Hohenzollerns had a strong army and had gained Eastern Pomerania, Magdeburg and Halberstadt in 1648.
Mecklenburg remained separate; the modern state polygon is assigned to Swedish Pomerania as a broad map approximation.
Sweden was a Baltic great power with Finland, Estonia, Ingria, Livonia and Pomerania, soon to be tested in the Great Northern War.
Charles II died childless in November 1700, which triggered the War of the Spanish Succession.
France had taken Artois and Nord (1659–1678) and Franche-Comté (1678). The rump Spanish Netherlands was a battleground.
Portugal regained independence from Spain in 1640 under the House of Braganza.

properties.leader: William III (stadtholder and king of England)
properties.info: The Dutch Republic was a leading commercial and naval power.
England had the Glorious Revolution (1688) and Parliament's supremacy. Union with Scotland followed in 1707.
Ulster was colonised by Protestant settlers (Plantation of Ulster) and Ireland was conquered by William III by 1691.
Scotland shared a monarch with England but had its own parliament until 1707.
Louis XIV's France was the leading power in Europe, having gained Alsace, Artois, Franche-Comté and Roussillon.
France annexed Artois (1659), Alsace (1648 and 1681), Franche-Comté and Nord (1678).
The Holy Roman Empire was a loose legal framework of German states, not a unified state. The Habsburgs held the imperial crown, but Hungary, Transylvania and Croatia lay outside it.
Habsburg Austria was the Empire's leading power after the victory over the Ottomans at Vienna (1683). The Empire lost Alsace to France.
Bohemia, with Moravia and Silesia, was a Habsburg crown land and an electorate within the Holy Roman Empire; the Habsburg Monarchy was a personal union of crowns under one ruler.

Croatia was part of the Hungarian crown under the Habsburgs. Much of Slavonia was recovered from the Ottomans at Karlowitz (1699). It was part of the Habsburg Monarchy (a personal union under one ruler) but outside the Holy Roman Empire.
After the Great Turkish War the Habsburgs controlled most of the Kingdom of Hungary. It was part of the Habsburg Monarchy (a personal union under one ruler) but outside the Holy Roman Empire.
The Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) gave the Habsburgs almost all of Ottoman Hungary except the Banat of Temesvár.
Transylvania passed under Habsburg rule in 1699 but kept its own diet and nobility. It was part of the Habsburg Monarchy (a personal union under one ruler) but outside the Holy Roman Empire.
Safavid Iran under Sultan Husayn (1694-1722) was a declining Shia empire, about to fall to the Afghans.

properties.label: Morocco
properties.info: The Alaouites replaced the Saadis in the 1660s and Moulay Ismail ruled a strong centralised Morocco.
Venice conquered the Morea in 1684–99 but lost Crete in 1669.
Scania, Halland and Blekinge passed from Denmark to Sweden in 1658 (Treaty of Roskilde); Gotland had been Swedish since 1645.

properties.label: Swedish Pomerania
properties.info: Sweden held Swedish Pomerania from 1648. This uses the whole modern Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania polygon, so it also includes Mecklenburg as a cartographic approximation.
The Banat of Temesvár stayed Ottoman until 1718.

1800.note: Europe around 1800: the French Republic has annexed the Austrian Netherlands and is reshaping the German and Italian states; Poland has been partitioned among Prussia, Austria and Russia; Russia has taken Sweden's Baltic provinces; the Holy Roman Empire still survives, but is under pressure.

properties.leader: Parma, Modena and Lucca under French and Austrian influence
properties.info: The small north Italian states were dominated by France and Austria after the Italian campaigns.
The Nogai steppe north of the Black Sea and the Caspian had come under Russian rule; Russia annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1783.
Kartli-Kakheti turned to Russia for protection in 1783 and was annexed in 1801.

properties.label: Qajar Iran
properties.info: The Qajar dynasty reunified Iran under Agha Mohammad Khan (1789-97); Fath-Ali Shah ruled from 1797.
Tuscany was a Habsburg-Lorraine grand duchy, occupied by France and turned into the Kingdom of Etruria in 1801.
The Republic of Venice fell to Napoleon in 1797 and was ceded to Austria by the Treaty of Campo Formio.
Portugal, with Brazil, was a British ally; the royal family fled to Brazil in 1807.
Morocco, under the Alaouite dynasty, was independent and isolated.

properties.leader: Christian VII (Crown Prince Frederick as regent)
properties.info: Denmark–Norway was a neutral trading power that held Norway, Iceland, Schleswig and Holstein.
Sweden had lost its Baltic provinces, but still held Finland and Swedish Pomerania; Gustav IV Adolf ruled 1792-1809 and lost Finland to Russia in 1809.
Selim III (1789-1807) attempted modernising reforms (the Nizam-i Cedid) while Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798.

properties.label: Russian Empire
properties.info: Russia expanded west after the partitions of Poland and took Estonia and Livonia from Sweden in 1721. Paul I ruled until his assassination in 1801.
Estonia passed to Russia after the Great Northern War (1721).
Livonia passed to Russia after the Great Northern War (1721).
Russia annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1783.
The Commonwealth was partitioned among Russia, Prussia and Austria in 1772, 1793 and 1795.

properties.label: Prussia
properties.info: Brandenburg and the Prussian lands were united under the Hohenzollerns. Prussia acquired extensive Polish territories in the partitions.
The former Duchy of Pomerania was divided between Prussia and Sweden; this polygon represents the Prussian part.
Mecklenburg remained separate; its modern combined polygon is assigned to Swedish Pomerania as a broad map approximation.
Swedish Pomerania remained Swedish until 1815. The modern Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania polygon also includes Mecklenburg.
Courland became a Russian governorate after the third partition of Poland in 1795.

properties.label: Batavian Republic
properties.info: The Dutch Republic was replaced by the French-backed Batavian Republic in 1795.

properties.label: Spain
properties.info: The Bourbon monarchy ruled Spain; Charles IV was king until his abdication in 1808.

properties.label: Sardinia
properties.info: The House of Savoy retained Sardinia after France occupied its mainland territories.

properties.label: Naples
properties.info: The Bourbon king ruled from Naples; the mainland kingdom was briefly occupied by France in 1799.

properties.label: Cisalpine Republic
properties.info: The French-backed Cisalpine Republic was re-established in 1800 after Napoleon's victory at Marengo.

properties.label: Ligurian Republic
properties.info: The French-backed Ligurian Republic replaced the Republic of Genoa in 1797.

properties.label: France
properties.info: The French Republic annexed Belgium in 1795 and dominated much of western Europe after the Revolutionary Wars.
The French Republic held these long-integrated regions and had annexed Artois, Alsace and Franche-Comté.
France annexed Savoy in 1792 and Piedmont in 1800; the House of Savoy retained Sardinia.

A loose legal framework of German states, dominated by Austria and Prussia. Francis II was its last emperor and it was dissolved in 1806. The Habsburgs' Hungary, Transylvania and Croatia lay outside it.

properties.label: Great Britain
properties.info: England and Scotland had been united as Great Britain since 1707; Ireland remained a separate kingdom until 1801.
Bohemia, with Moravia and Silesia, was a Habsburg crown land inside the Holy Roman Empire; the Habsburg Monarchy was a personal union of crowns under Francis II (Emperor of Austria from 1804).
Croatia belonged to the Hungarian crown under the Habsburgs. It was part of the Habsburg Monarchy (a personal union under one ruler) but outside the Holy Roman Empire.
The Kingdom of Hungary was ruled by Francis II as king. It was part of the Habsburg Monarchy (a personal union under one ruler) but outside the Holy Roman Empire.
Transylvania was a distinct principality under the Hungarian crown. It was part of the Habsburg Monarchy (a personal union under one ruler) but outside the Holy Roman Empire.
Moldavia was an Ottoman tributary principality ruled by hospodars appointed from Constantinople.
France annexed the Austrian Netherlands in 1795 and occupied the left bank of the Rhine; Luxembourg was also incorporated.
Russia annexed Lithuania and Courland through the partitions of Poland.
Prussia received much of northern and central Poland in the partitions of 1772, 1793 and 1795.
Austria acquired Galicia and adjoining southern Polish lands in the partitions of Poland.
Russia took Lithuania, Belarus and much of present-day Ukraine through the partitions of Poland.
The Habsburg Monarchy acquired the Banat from the Ottomans in 1718.

1815.note: Europe 1815 after the Congress of Vienna: Austrian Empire, enlarged Prussia, German Confederation states, Congress Poland, United Netherlands, Sweden-Norway.

properties.label: Netherlands
properties.info: The Congress of Vienna created a united kingdom of the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg under the House of Orange.
A Habsburg crown land: Francis I ruled it as king or archduke, in personal union with the Austrian Empire.

properties.label: Switzerland
properties.info: The Swiss Confederation was restored in 1815 with 22 cantons and declared permanently neutral.

properties.label: France
properties.info: The Bourbons were restored in 1814-15 after Napoleon's fall, and France was reduced to roughly its 1790 borders.

properties.label: Tuscany
properties.info: Habsburg-Lorraine Tuscany was restored in 1814.
A Habsburg crown land: Francis I ruled it as king or archduke, in personal union with the Austrian Empire.

properties.label: Prussia
properties.info: Prussia was restored in 1815 and gained the Rhineland, Westphalia, Posen, northern Saxony and Swedish Pomerania; it was now the leading power in the German Confederation.

properties.label: Sardinia
properties.info: Restored in 1814, Sardinia regained Savoy and Nice and gained Genoa and Liguria at the Congress of Vienna.
Sicily remained under Bourbon rule through the Napoleonic era, protected by the British; merged with Naples in 1816.

properties.label: Spain
properties.info: Spain was restored under Ferdinand VII after the Peninsular War (1808-14); its American colonies were in revolt.

properties.info: The Papal States were restored in 1814-15 under Pius VII, including the Legations of Bologna and Ferrara.
Moldavia, reduced after Russia annexed Bessarabia in 1812, was an Ottoman vassal under a Phanariot hospodar.
A Habsburg crown land: Francis I ruled it as king or archduke, in personal union with the Austrian Empire.

properties.label: Thuringian states
properties.info: Thuringia was split into many small Saxon duchies and principalities, which joined the German Confederation in 1815.

properties.label: Saxony
properties.info: Saxony, a loyal ally of Napoleon, lost about half its territory to Prussia in 1815.

properties.label: Hesse
properties.info: Hesse was divided between the Electorate of Hesse-Kassel and the Grand Duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt, both members of the German Confederation.

properties.label: Hanover
properties.info: Hanover became a kingdom in 1814 and was in personal union with the British crown, gaining East Frisia and Hildesheim.

properties.label: Württemberg and Baden
properties.info: Napoleon's allies Württemberg (kingdom) and Baden (grand duchy) kept their enlarged territories and joined the German Confederation in 1815.

properties.label: Bavaria
properties.info: Bavaria became a kingdom in 1806 under Napoleon and in 1815 joined the German Confederation, gaining the Palatinate in 1816.

properties.label: Austrian Empire
properties.info: The Austrian Empire (proclaimed 1804; Austria-Hungary only came in 1867) included Bohemia, Hungary, Croatia, Transylvania and Galicia, and regained Lombardy-Venetia, Tyrol, Illyria and Galicia at the Congress of Vienna, but gave up the Holy Roman crown in 1806 and the Austrian Netherlands. Bohemia, Hungary, Croatia and Transylvania were ruled in personal union.
These lands remained Ottoman.

properties.label: Congress Poland
properties.info: The Kingdom of Poland, created in 1815 from the Duchy of Warsaw, had its own constitution but was ruled by the Russian tsar as king.
Malta was taken from the French in 1800 and confirmed as British in 1814.

properties.label: Modena
properties.info: The Austrian Archduke Francis IV ruled Modena, Reggio and Massa-Carrara.

properties.label: Lucca
properties.info: Lucca was a small Bourbon duchy under Marie Louise until 1824, when it was absorbed into Tuscany.
Naples was restored under Ferdinand IV after Murat's fall; the two kingdoms were merged as the Two Sicilies in 1816.

properties.realm: United States of the Ionian Islands
properties.label: Ionian Islands
properties.info: The Ionian Islands became a British protectorate in 1815.
Armenia and Nakhchivan were still Persian until 1828.

properties.label: Sweden–Norway
properties.info: Sweden lost Finland to Russia (1809) and Swedish Pomerania, but gained Norway in 1814 in a personal union under one king.

1871.note: Europe in 1871: the German Empire is proclaimed, Italy has just taken Rome, Austria-Hungary is a dual monarchy, France is a republic, and the Balkans, Bosnia and Cyprus are still Ottoman.

properties.info: The Third Republic was proclaimed in September 1870 after Napoleon III fell at Sedan; France lost Alsace and part of Lorraine and put down the Paris Commune in 1871.
Italy was almost unified: Venetia was gained in 1866 and Rome was taken from the Pope in 1870 (capital from 1871); Trento and Trieste were still Austrian.
Morocco was an independent sultanate under Muhammad IV (1859-73), under growing European pressure.
Russia under Alexander II had freed the serfs in 1861 and was expanding in Central Asia and the Caucasus; Poland, the Baltic provinces and Finland were under the tsar.
Persia was ruled by Naser al-Din Shah of the Qajar dynasty, balancing between Russia and Britain.
After the Revolution of 1868 ousted Isabella II, Spain was ruled by Amadeo of Savoy (1870-73), followed by the First Republic.
Portugal under Luís I (1861-89) was a constitutional monarchy with African colonies.
France had ruled Algeria since 1830; Tunisia was still a nominally Ottoman beylik until the protectorate of 1881.

The Ottoman Empire still held the whole Balkans from Bosnia and Bulgaria to Thessaly and Macedonia, plus Anatolia, the Levant, Iraq, the Hejaz, Cyprus and Libya; Serbia and Romania were autonomous vassals.
The Kingdom of the Netherlands under William III (1849-90).
Luxembourg was a neutral grand duchy (since 1867) in personal union with the Netherlands.
The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles on 18 January 1871 under Wilhelm I of Prussia, uniting the North German Confederation with the southern states; Alsace was annexed from France.
Sweden and Norway were in a personal union under Charles XV (d. 1872, succeeded by Oscar II); Norway kept its own constitution and parliament.
Finland was a grand duchy under the Russian tsar since 1809, with its own diet.
The Dual Monarchy of Austria and Hungary was created by the Compromise of 1867 under Franz Joseph I; Bosnia was still Ottoman.
Greece received the Ionian Islands from Britain in 1864; Thessaly, Epirus, Macedonia and Crete were still Ottoman.
Montenegro was a small mountain principality around Cetinje under Nicholas I; it was recognised as independent only in 1878, when it roughly doubled in size.
Belgium became independent in 1830; Leopold II reigned from 1865.
Denmark lost Schleswig-Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864 but kept Iceland and the Faroe Islands.
The United Kingdom was the leading industrial and naval power, with Gladstone as prime minister; Queen Victoria reigned until 1901.

properties.label: Ottoman Empire
properties.info: Bulgaria was still a set of Ottoman provinces; the autonomous principality came only in 1878.
Bosnia and Herzegovina were Ottoman until Austria-Hungary occupied them in 1878.
Cyprus was Ottoman until Britain took over its administration in 1878.
Thessaly was Ottoman until it was ceded to Greece in 1881.
Egypt was a semi-autonomous Ottoman khedivate; Isma’il opened the Suez Canal in 1869 and ran up huge debts.
Serbia was an autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty; it gained independence and the Niš region only in 1878, and became a kingdom in 1882.
Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859 and Carol I of Hohenzollern became prince in 1866; Romania was still under Ottoman suzerainty and Dobruja was Ottoman.
These districts were Ottoman until Montenegro took them in 1878.
The Bay of Kotor belonged to the Austrian Kingdom of Dalmatia.

properties.label: Tunis
properties.info: Tunisia was a nominally Ottoman beylik, effectively autonomous and deep in debt; France made it a protectorate in 1881.
These districts (including the Sanjak of Novi Pazar) were Ottoman until Serbia took them in 1878 (Novi Pazar until 1912).
Dobruja was Ottoman until it passed to Romania in 1878.

1900.note: Europe c. 1900: German and Italian unification, Austria-Hungary, independent Balkan states, French North Africa, Sweden-Norway union.

properties.info: Morocco was still independent under the Alaouite dynasty, but under growing French and Spanish pressure.

properties.label: Netherlands
properties.info: The Kingdom of the Netherlands; Queen Wilhelmina succeeded in 1890.
Italy was unified between 1859 and 1870 under the House of Savoy, with Rome as capital from 1871.
Russia ruled from Finland to the Pacific; Poland, the Baltic provinces, Ukraine, Bessarabia and the Caucasus were all incorporated.
The Dual Monarchy of Austria and Hungary (1867) ruled Bohemia, Galicia, Croatia, Transylvania and the Slovene lands; Bosnia was occupied from 1878.
Denmark had lost Norway (1814) and Schleswig-Holstein (1864) but kept Iceland and the Faroe Islands.
Denmark had lost Norway (1814) and Schleswig-Holstein (1864) but kept Iceland and the Faroe Islands.

properties.label: Hungary
properties.info: Hungary declared itself a republic in November 1918. Its postwar borders had not yet been settled.

properties.label: Czechoslovakia
properties.info: Czechoslovakia declared independence in October 1918, joining the Czech lands and Slovakia. Borders were provisional.

properties.realm: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
properties.label: Yugoslavia
properties.info: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was proclaimed in December 1918, uniting Serbia, Montenegro and South Slavic lands of the former Austria-Hungary. Borders were provisional.

properties.label: Poland
properties.info: Poland was restored as an independent state in November 1918. Its borders remained disputed and provisional.

properties.label: Romania
properties.info: Romania claimed Transylvania and united with Bessarabia in 1918; these borders were not yet internationally settled.
Italian forces occupied Trentino, South Tyrol, Gorizia and Trieste in November 1918; formal borders were settled later.
France resumed control of Alsace-Lorraine after the German armistice in November 1918.

properties.label: Finland
properties.info: Finland declared independence from Russia in December 1917. The proposed Finnish king abdicated in December 1918, leaving Mannerheim as regent.

properties.label: Estonia
properties.info: Estonia had declared independence in February 1918, although foreign troops and the ensuing War of Independence made control contested.

properties.label: Latvia
properties.info: Latvia declared independence in November 1918. German forces and the ongoing War of Independence made control contested.

properties.label: Lithuania
properties.info: Lithuania declared independence in February 1918; German occupation and subsequent fighting left control contested.

properties.label: Ukraine
properties.info: The Ukrainian People's Republic was restored in December 1918 after the Hetmanate fell. Its territory was contested in the civil war.

properties.label: Georgia
properties.info: Georgia declared independence in May 1918 after the collapse of the Russian Empire.

properties.label: Armenia
properties.info: The First Republic of Armenia declared independence in May 1918 amid war and disputed borders.

properties.label: Azerbaijan
properties.info: The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic declared independence in May 1918; its borders remained contested.

1939.note: Europe on 1 September 1939, immediately before the German invasion of Poland. Austria, the Sudetenland and Memel had been annexed by Germany; Bohemia and Moravia were a German protectorate; Slovakia was independent; Albania was under Italian rule. Poland, the Baltic states and Finland were still independent. Modern administrative regions are approximate territorial proxies.
